ICML Sponsor Hotel & Function Space Requests – Required Process All guest room requests, including individual reservations and room blocks, must be submitted through the official ICML Housing Team. Availability is managed on a first-come, first-served basis, and this process is required to protect conference commitments and contracted agreements. All meeting and function space requests must be reviewed and approved by the ICML team before any arrangements can be made to ensure there are no conflicts with the official conference program. Please do not contact hotels directly. Hotels will refer all ICML-related requests back to the conference team, which will only delay the process. If your request does not conflict with the official program, we will work to assist you as quickly as possible. Following the official process is the fastest and most effective path forward. About the Conference The International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML) is the premier gathering of professionals dedicated to the advancement of the branch of artificial intelligence known as machine learning. ICML is globally renowned for presenting and publishing cutting-edge research on all aspects of machine learning used in closely related areas like artificial intelligence, statistics and data science, as well as important application areas such as machine vision, computational biology, speech recognition, and robotics. ICML is one of the fastest growing artificial intelligence conferences in the world. Participants at ICML span a wide range of backgrounds, from academic and industrial researchers, to entrepreneurs and engineers, to graduate students and postdocs.

items.content: The European AI Office supports the development and adoption of trustworthy Artificial Intelligence (AI) solutions, while protecting people against risks. The European AI Office was established within the European Commission as the foundation for a single AI governance system. It supports the EU approach to AI , playing a key role in implementing the AI Act – especially for general-purpose AI (GPAI) – guaranteeing the health, safety and fundamental rights of people and providing legal certainty to businesses. It also enforces the rules for GPAI models and supports the governance bodies in Member States in their tasks. This is underpinned by the powers given to the Commission by the AI Act, including the ability to conduct evaluations of GPAI models, request information and measures from model providers, and apply sanctions. The AI Office also promotes an innovative ecosystem of trustworthy AI , to reap the societal and economic benefits. It ensures a strategic, coherent and effective European approach to AI at international level , becoming a global reference point. The Structure of the AI Office The AI Office employs more than 125 staff, including technology specialists, administrative assistants, lawyers, policy specialists, and economists. It has 6 units and 2 advisers, reflecting its mandate: “Excellence in AI and Robotics” - unit A1 “Regulation and Compliance” - unit A2 “AI Safety” - unit A3 “AI Innovation and Policy Coordination” - unit A4 “AI for Societal Good” - unit A5 "AI in Health and Life Science" - unit A6 Lead Scientific Adviser International Affairs Adviser Tasks of the AI Office Supporting the AI Act and enforcing general-purpose AI rules The AI Office makes use of its expertise to support the implementation and enforcement of the AI Act by: Contributing to the coherent application of the AI Act across the Member States, including the set-up of advisory bodies at EU level, facilitating support and information exchange Developing tools, methodologies and benchmarks for evaluating capabilities and reach of general-purpose AI models, and classifying models with systemic risks Drawing up state-of-the-art codes of practice to detail out rules, in cooperation with leading AI developers, the scientific community and other experts Preparing guidance and guidelines, implementing and delegated acts , and other tools to support effective implementation of the AI Act and monitor compliance with the regulation Investigating possible infringements of the rules, including inspections, requests for technical documentation and access to models in order to assess models' capabilities Requesting providers to take corrective action and, in case of infringement, restrict the public availability of a model and issue direct fines for non-compliance Strengthening the development and use of trustworthy AI The AI Office, in collaboration with relevant public and private actors and the startup community, contributes to fostering trustworthy AI across the EU by: Advancing actions and policies to reap the societal and economic benefits of AI across the EU Providing advice on best practices and enabling ready-access to AI sandboxes, real-world testing and other European support structures for AI uptake Encouraging innovative ecosystems of trustworthy AI to enhance the EU’s competitiveness and economic growth Aiding the Commission in leveraging the use of transformative AI tools and reinforcing AI literacy Fostering international cooperation At international level, the AI Office contributes to a strategic, coherent, and effective EU approach, by: Promoting the EU’s approach to trustworthy AI , including collaboration with similar institutions worldwide Fostering international cooperation and governance on AI, contributing to a global approach to AI Supporting the development and implementation of international agreements on AI Cooperation with institutions, experts and stakeholders The AI Office collaborates with Member States and the wider expert community through dedicated platforms: The European Artificial Intelligence Board (AI Board) is a key advisory body supported by the AI Office that includes representatives from each EU Member States and the European Centre for Algorithmic Transparency (ECAT). The AI Board’s primary role is to ensure the effective implementation of the AI Act across the EU by coordinating national authorities, sharing technical and regulatory expertise and providing advice on AI policy, innovation, and international partnerships. The Scientific Panel of independent experts ensures a strong link with the scientific community. Further technical expertise is gathered in an Advisory Forum , representing a balanced selection of stakeholders, including industry, startups and Small and Medium-sized Enterprises (SMEs), academia, think tanks and civil society. The AI Office also oversees the AI Pact , which allows businesses to engage with the Commission and other stakeholders to share best practices and join activities. This engagement has started before the AI Act entered into force and allows businesses to plan ahead and prepare for the full implementation of the AI Act. To stay up to date and register, check the AI Pact events . The Apply AI Alliance is the main coordination forum bringing together AI providers, industry leaders, academia and the public sector to ensure policy actions are grounded in the real-world needs. Closely connected to the Alliance, an AI Observatory will track AI trends and assess impact of AI in specific sectors. Initiatives promoting the development and adoption of AI The AI Office actively supports innovators through policies and initiatives that spur growth across the EU: The AI Continent action plan , launched in April 2025, explains how to harness the untapped potential of EU researchers and industries, turning EU strengths – such as unparalleled talent and strong traditional industries – into AI accelerators. The plan promotes economic growth and competitiveness in areas such as healthcare, cars, science. The Apply AI Strategy , launched in October 2025, complements the action plan. It aims to boost AI adoption and innovation across Europe, particularly among SMEs. It is designed to enhance the competitiveness of strategic sectors and strengthen the EU’s tech sovereignty. In June 2026, the 'AI omnibus' (part of the Digital Simplification Package ) was adopted, introducing targeted amendments to the AI Act to ensure the rules remain clear, simple, and innovation-friendly. The amendments entered into force on 27 July. The ‘ GenAI4EU ' initiative, part of the 2024 AI innovation package , contributes to the development of novel use cases and emerging applications in 14 industrial sectors and the public sector. Other initiatives aimed at boosting the development and uptake of AI are: AI Factories Testing and Experimentation Facilities (TEFS) and sandboxes European Digital Innovation Hubs (EDIHs) AI skills and literacy Job opportunities and collaboration The AI Office recruits talent from a wide range of backgrounds for policy, technical and legal roles and administrative support. To apply, complete the Expression of Interest Form . For inquiries, please contact us at the following addresses: Recruitment: CNECT-AIOFFICE-RECRUITMENT@ec.europa.eu General Inquiries: CNECT-AIOFFICE@ec.europa.eu Important: These email addresses are for inquiries only. Applications must be submitted through the dedicated form, not via email. Quick Links Any question on the AI Act? Affiliation: UIUC Wei Zuo Affiliation: Microsoft Walid Krichene Affiliation: Microsoft Tong Zhang Affiliation: UIUC Li Zhang Affiliation: Affiliation: Microsoft Abstract Speculative decoding accelerates large language model (LLM) inference by employing a lightweight draft model to propose draft tokens and allowing the target model to verify the new tokens in parallel to improve inference-time compute utilization. The speedup relies on the acceptance probability of draft tokens in target verification, which is directly related to the gap ‖ p − q ‖ 1 \left\|p-q\right\|_{1} between the target distribution p p and the draft distribution q q . In this paper, we study draft calibration of speculative decoding to improve the speedup of speculative decoding, where we employ post-hoc methods to calibrate the draft distribution to mitigate the distribution gap. We observe that though current community open-source draft models may learn the top candidate token correctly, they are generally underconfident compared to the target model, suggesting a consistent distribution mismatch. To mitigate the effect of this mismatch on the acceptance rate of the draft models, we try various post-hoc calibration methods, including standard temperature scaling and token-wise calibration. Our results suggest that a standard temperature scaling applied to the draft distribution improves the acceptance length by up to approximately 10% with almost no additional cost across different tasks. Throughput analysis further verifies that this improvement in serving efficiency. Analysis of more general calibration methods reveals further potential room for improvement. 1 Introduction Current state-of-the-art large language models (LLMs) generate text in an autoregressive way, which runs one new forward pass to generate one next token recursively. This nature of LLM serving results in an insufficient use of parallelism in modern computational resources like GPUs. Speculative decoding ( Leviathan et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2023 ) is considered a valid solution to mitigate this fundamental serving inefficiency: at each inference time, a lightweight draft model first proposes a draft block that contains several draft tokens in a row, and the target model (the serving model) verifies all the draft tokens through one forward pass. Thanks to the rejection sampling design at the verification stage, speculative decoding perfectly preserves the target model distribution while accelerating inference by lowering the number of target model forward passes to improve compute utilization and ultimately serving efficiency. The speedup achieved by speculative decoding fundamentally relies on the acceptance rate of each draft token, i.e., the probability that a draft token can be accepted by the target model verification, which has a closed-form representation 1 − 1 2 ​ ‖ p − q ‖ 1 1-\frac{1}{2}\left\|p-q\right\|_{1} on target distribution p p and draft distribution q q ( Leviathan et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2023 ) . Therefore, a clear target to improve speculative decoding is that we not only desire the draft model to learn top candidates for each token well, but also to minimize this ℓ 1 \ell_{1} distribution gap. This formula motivates a connection to confidence calibration ( Guo et al., 2017 ; Wang, 2023 ) , where predicted probabilities should match empirical correctness frequencies rather than merely identify the top candidate class. In speculative decoding, the formulation can be more straightforward: since the goal is to improve the acceptance rate, we consider the target distribution as the ground truth, and calibrate the draft distribution to mitigate this ℓ 1 \ell_{1} distribution gap and thus improve the acceptance rate. From this perspective, we may improve speculative decoding not only in training time through algorithm and architecture modifications ( Cai et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2024c ; Li et al., 2024b ; Li et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2026 ; Cheng et al., 2026 ) , but also after training by calibrating the draft distribution better, which we study systematically across draft architectures. In this paper, we study this draft calibration idea of speculative decoding, mainly on post-hoc methods adjusting the draft distribution q q to mitigate the ℓ 1 \ell_{1} distribution gap at inference time when using chain draft generation. In existing literature and community speculative decoding serving frameworks, one usually shares the inference settings as the target model without any modification when chain generating draft tokens. However, as we observe across community open-source draft models on different tasks, this choice may not be optimal because of the existence of a systematic mismatch between the draft and target models under the original setup. More specifically, the draft models tend to be underconfident compared to the target model when using the same generation settings, even though they have learned the top candidates correctly, revealing a consistent distribution gap. To mitigate this gap and improve the speculative decoding speedup, we consider multiple calibration methods applied to the draft distribution, and show that a standard temperature scaling ( Guo et al., 2017 ) for the draft distribution can significantly mitigate the gap and improve the overall accepted length by up to around 10% with almost no additional cost. We also further study Dirichlet scaling ( Kull et al., 2019 ) , a generalization of temperature scaling, and token-adaptive calibration methods, which apply more fine-grained adjustments to the draft distribution. Analysis of the optimal choices for these methods reveals further potential room of improvement with draft calibration, but currently the tried post-hoc methods still cannot capture it well. Our key contributions include: • We present the underconfident tendency of draft models compared to target models, forming a consistent distribution mismatch that affects acceptance rate. • We study the problem from the draft calibration perspective and apply different calibration methods to mitigate the systematic distribution gap, showing that standard temperature scaling can already significantly improve the acceptance rate across different settings. • We further examine more general calibration methods and reveal that there is room for improvements with token-adaptive calibration methods through a trajectory replay analysis framework, though the current pure post-hoc methods may not be able to capture it. 2 Backgrounds and Understanding of Draft Calibration Speculative decoding. To accelerate the inference of a large model, referred to as the target model, speculative decoding ( Leviathan et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2023 ) incorporates a lightweight draft model and follows a draft-then-verify pipeline. At inference time, given a prefix sequence x 1 , … , x t x_{1},\dots,x_{t} , we let the draft model generate K K draft tokens in a row, then feed all the draft tokens to the target model to run a forward pass to verify them. The verification process goes one by one, i.e., if one draft token is not accepted by the verification, we abandon all of the subsequent draft tokens. For each draft token x t x_{t} at position t t with draft distribution q q and target distribution p p on vocabulary 𝒱 \mathcal{V} , we do a rejection sampling process: we accept the token if p ⁡ ( x t ) ≥ q ⁡ ( x t ) p(x_{t})\geq q(x_{t}) , otherwise we reject it with probability 1 − p ⁡ ( x t ) q ⁡ ( x t ) 1-\frac{p(x_{t})}{q(x_{t})} and resample a new token from an adjusted distribution p ′ ​ ( x ) = normalize ⁡ ( max ⁡ ( 0 , p ⁡ ( x ) − q ⁡ ( x ) ) ) p^{\prime}(x)=\mathrm{normalize}(\max(0,p(x)-q(x))) . We can compute the expected acceptance rate of each draft token from the sampling strategy: ℙ ⁡ ( x t ​ is accepted ) = ∑ x ∈ 𝒱 min ⁡ ( p ⁡ ( x ) , q ⁡ ( x ) ) = 1 − 1 2 ​ ‖ p − q ‖ 1 . \displaystyle{\mathbb{P}}(x_{t}\text{ is accepted})=\sum_{x\in\mathcal{V}}\min(p(x),q(x))=1-\frac{1}{2}\left\|p-q\right\|_{1}. (1) Clearly, mitigating this ℓ 1 \ell_{1} gap between draft and target models directly improves acceptance rate and the effectiveness of speculative decoding. Confidence calibration and draft calibration. Confidence calibration has been an important field for deep learning and trustworthy AI ( Guo et al., 2017 ) . In a classification problem of feature label pairs ( X , y ) (X,y) , calibration measures how much a model’s predicted probability matches the true correctness likelihood. More formally, a classifier model that maps the feature X X to a probability simplex q q is perfectly calibrated if ℙ ⁡ ( y = y i | q ⁡ ( y i ) = q i ) = q i {\mathbb{P}}(y=y_{i}|q(y_{i})=q_{i})=q_{i} for class i i . Post-hoc methods fit a calibration map on held-out data while keeping the predictor fixed, ranging from histogram binning and isotonic regression to temperature and Dirichlet scaling ( Guo et al., 2017 ; Kull et al., 2019 ) . Given the goal of improving acceptance of draft tokens for speculative decoding, we can also consider it from the calibration perspective, where we try to mitigate the distribution gap between the draft distribution and target distribution, and we term it draft calibration in this paper. Compared to the confidence calibration problem, the idea is more straightforward: we have the ground truth target distribution after verification for each draft token, and can simply adopt acceptance performance as the evaluation metric for draft calibration. In this paper, we will focus on post-hoc methods to help calibrate the draft distribution better, which preserves the lossless property of speculative decoding, keeping the target distribution unchanged as long as the calibrated distribution q q is employed consistently in drafting and rejection sampling stages ( Leviathan et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2023 ) . Relation to draft tree methods. We focus on chain drafting in this paper, motivated by large-scale serving, where we handle many concurrent requests that compete for verification compute. Draft trees increase candidate coverage by proposing multiple continuations at each draft position ( Li et al., 2024b ; Li et al., 2026b ) , but their additional branches also introduce more verification costs. This tradeoff becomes more restrictive as batch size grows: Liu et al. (2026) , for example, find that a 21-token tree becomes slower than autoregressive decoding at batch size 64 across their evaluated workloads, while the three-token chain retains a speedup. Likewise, the concurrent-serving study in Li et al. (2026b) also reports largely reduced tree node budgets to keep the effectiveness of the draft tree with a batch size of 32. The evidence suggests that the benefits of draft trees may be limited in large-scale serving, where the batch size can be up to hundreds. We therefore keep our focus on how much acceptance can be improved by calibrating the draft distribution. 3 Related Work Speculative decoding. Early blockwise and speculative methods amortize verification over multiple candidate tokens ( Stern et al., 2018 ; Xia et al., 2023 ) , while speculative sampling pairs a lightweight drafter with parallel target verification to preserve the target distribution ( Leviathan et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2023 ) . Subsequent work improves draft efficiency and alignment through alternative backbones and distillation ( Choi et al., 2025 ; Zhou et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ) , and expands candidate coverage through tree-based verification ( Miao et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2024b ; Li et al., 2026b ) . Medusa, EAGLE, and related draft-head designs introduce additional decoding heads or a lightweight draft layer conditioned on target features instead of standalone draft models ( Cai et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2024c ; Ankner et al., 2024 ) , and the latter state-of-the-art methods follow this design, including self-speculation methods ( Zhang et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2024 ) and EAGLE-3 ( Li et al., 2025 ) . ParallelSpec, P-EAGLE, DFlash, and related parallel drafters reduce sequential drafting overhead by predicting multiple positions in parallel, including through block-diffusion drafting ( Xiao et al., 2024 ; Hui et al., 2026 ; An et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2026 ) . Built upon the parallelism idea, DSpark augments a parallel backbone with lightweight autoregressive correction and confidence-based verification scheduling ( Cheng et al., 2026 ) . Confidence calibration. Confidence calibration aligns predicted confidence with empirical correctness and has been studied through post-hoc maps and calibration-aware training ( Guo et al., 2017 ; Kumar et al., 2018 ; Mukhoti et al., 2020 ; Wang, 2023 ) . Post-hoc approaches include binning, parametric scaling, and their compositions ( Naeini et al., 2015 ; Kull et al., 2017 ; Kull et al., 2019 ; Kumar et al., 2019 ; Zhang et al., 2020 ; Ding et al., 2021 ) . More recent studies also examine token-adaptive temperature scaling for language models ( Desai and Durrett, 2020 ; Xie et al., 2024 ) . Post-hoc draft calibration in speculative decoding. Draft calibration is largely unexplored in the literature, and prior works with temperature and distribution adjustment address several distinct objectives ( Wang et al., 2025 ; Ouyang et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ; Berdoz et al., 2026 ; Zhou et al., 2026 ) , with the following works as examples. SubSpec sharpens draft probabilities to improve cumulative-probability ranking in deep draft trees for offloaded inference with a greedy target, but does not systematically study the draft calibration ( Wang et al., 2025 ) . Ouyang et al. (2024) study the interaction between the training data of the draft model and decoding temperatures, but does not consider differentiating the temperature of the draft model. Other work calibrates confidence for control decisions: SpecBound temperature-scales shallow-layer outputs for early exit, while DSpark calibrates predicted prefix acceptance for verification scheduling ( Wen and Feng, 2026 ; Cheng et al., 2026 ) . Differently, we focus on systematically studying the distribution gap between draft and target models and methods to mitigate the gap. 4 Underconfident Draft Models We start from examining the current popular open-source draft models’ distribution gap compared to the corresponding target models, which forms the basis of applying post-hoc draft calibration methods. While Guo et al. (2017) discovers that modern neural networks tend to be overconfident in the choice they make, we find that draft models are generally underconfident compared to target models, admitting a consistently lower probability for top candidates. In other words, the draft distribution is generally flatter. 4.1 Experiment Settings & Metrics Unless otherwise specified, we employ the following experiment settings for speculative decoding evaluation throughout the paper. We evaluate nine target–draft pairs using community open-source EAGLE-3 ( Li et al., 2025 ) , DFlash ( Chen et al., 2026 ) , and DSpark ( Cheng et al., 2026 ) checkpoints for our evaluation. Target Models include GPT-OSS-120B, Gemma-4-31B-IT, and the Qwen series. Table 5 lists the exact pairings, checkpoint links, and chain lengths, which we generally follow the recommended settings. We use eight benchmarks spanning math (GSM8K, MATH-500, AIME 2025), code (HumanEval, MBPP, LiveCodeBench), and chat (MT-Bench, Arena-Hard v2), with sources and citations listed in Table 6 . We use low-reasoning/no-thinking chat template in the experiments unless otherwise specified. The experiments are done on SpecForge ( Li et al., 2026a ) /SGLang ( Zheng et al., 2024 ) stack with independent draft-temperature control and use chain proposals and rejection sampling with the calibrated draft probabilities. The temperature for the target model is fixed at T t = 1 T_{t}=1 , and generation is capped at 2,048 tokens. Each model pair keeps its chain length fixed across calibration methods. Please refer to more evaluation details in Appendix A . We use the accepted length as our evaluation metric: output tokens committed per verification round, including the bonus token. We aggregate rounds within each task and report an equal-weight mean across tasks. Distribution diagnostics average over eligible draft positions, where all preceding proposals in the block were accepted. 4.2 Draft Models can learn top candidates well, but are underconfident We use the same inference setup for draft and target models as default in this section. Generally consistent top candidates. We start from examining how consistent the top candidates learned by the draft model are with the target model. In Figure 1 , we show the overlap percentage between the top-k candidates of draft and target distributions regardless of order, i.e., how many of the top-k candidates are the same between target and draft models. We can observe that the draft model can learn around 70% or more for the top-1 token, showing its capability for catching the top candidate in the target distribution. The correctness tends to decrease, but it still remains more than 40% up to the top 16 candidates. Figure 1: The overlap percentage of top-k candidates in target and draft distributions on three different draft models, where k = 1 , 2 , 4 , 8 , 16 k=1,2,4,8,16 . Underconfident draft model. While the top candidates are generally learned correctly, we observe a consistent gap between the draft and target distributions. Figure 2 shows the probability draft and target distributions give the top-1 candidate when they agree, and the entropy of the distributions. Across different tasks and state-of-the-art speculative decoding algorithms, there exists a consistent gap between the top-1 probability of draft and target distributions, even if the draft model predicts it correctly – the draft model is underconfident about its top candidate choice compared to the target distribution. The consistently higher entropy also provides further evidence that the draft distribution is generally flatter than the target distribution. To conclude, the draft models are overall underconfident compared to the target model. Remark 1 (Why this distribution gap exists) . This consistent distribution gap is actually surprising since the draft distribution should be trained to match the target distribution. We hypothesize that this may be related to the limited capacity of draft models, making it hard to learn a sharp distribution as the target model. The settings of the training recipe could also be a potential reason for this. As discussed in Section 5.1 , DeepSeek-trained draft models have a smaller draft-target distribution gap across different speculative decoding algorithms. For example, the KL loss employed by the standard draft model training pipeline may also contribute to this, since it biases from the ℓ 1 \ell_{1} distribution gap ( Samarin et al., 2026 ) . Figure 2: Top-1 candidate probability when the top candidate agrees (first row) and entropy (second row) of draft and target distributions on three different draft models. 5 Draft Calibration Methods Recall that the acceptance probability of a draft token can be computed by A = 1 − 1 2 ​ ‖ p − q ‖ 1 A=1-\frac{1}{2}\left\|p-q\right\|_{1} that is directly related to the draft and target distribution gap. Observing the underconfident and flat draft distribution, it is natural to consider post-hoc calibration to mitigate its gap with the target distribution to improve the acceptance performance. In this section, we examine from standard general calibration methods to token-wise adaptive calibration, and show that the simple and popular temperature scaling already gives a significant improvement in accepted length. 5.1 Temperature Scaling Temperature scaling ( Guo et al., 2017 ) has become a standard default calibration and LLM inference technique. Given logits z ∈ ℝ V z\in{\mathbb{R}}^{V} and temperature T T , the corresponding probability distribution is: p cal = softmax ⁡ ( z T ) , i.e., ​ [ p T ] i = e z i / T ∑ j = 1 V e z j / T ​ for any ​ i ∈ [ V ] . \displaystyle p_{\mathrm{cal}}=\mathrm{softmax}\left(\frac{z}{T}\right),\text{ i.e., }[p_{T}]_{i}=\frac{\mathrm{e}^{z_{i}/T}}{\sum_{j=1}^{V}\mathrm{e}^{z_{j}/T}}\text{ for any }i\in[V]. From this formula, it is clear that lowering the temperature leads to a sharper distribution while keeping the rank of candidates the same. For speculative decoding, we actually have two temperature parameters: T t T_{t} for the target model that affects the quality of the generated text, which is considered fixed in the speculative decoding problem, and T d T_{d} for the draft model that only affects the draft distribution q q , treated as an independent calibration parameter allowed to be different from T t T_{t} . As presented in Section 4 , the draft models are consistently underconfident with this default choice T d = T t T_{d}=T_{t} when T t = 1 T_{t}=1 . Since lowering T d T_{d} leads to higher top candidate probability and sharper draft temperature, our first trial for post-hoc calibration is tuning this T d T_{d} as a hyperparameter to check whether it helps mitigate the distribution gap, where we employ accepted length as the evaluation metric because of the direct relation between acceptance rate and distribution gap. The following experiments are conducted under the specified settings in Section 4.1 . Figure 3: The accepted length across different models and speculative decoding algorithms when different draft temperatures are employed. The black line represents the average accepted length when the draft temperature is employed across all the tasks, and the bronze star means the optimal accepted length when we select the optimal temperature for each task. We specifically highlight their values and the baseline T d = 1 T_{d}=1 for reference. Temperature scaling shows improvements across models and tasks. We apply temperature scaling to the draft model to adjust its distribution with a grid of T d ∈ { 0 , 0.2 , 0.4 , 0.6 , 0.8 , 1 , 1.2 } T_{d}\in\{0,0.2,0.4,0.6,0.8,1,1.2\} while keeping the temperature for the target model T t = 1 T_{t}=1 . Following the settings in Section 4.1 , we are using no/low thinking mode for the models. We summarize the key observations on the results presented in Figure 3 . • Across all the considered settings, accepted length shows a clear peak when T d ∈ [ 0 , 0.8 ] T_{d}\in[0,0.8] . This is consistent with the observation that the draft models are generally underconfident, since T d < 1 T_{d}<1 sharpens the draft distribution and achieves better performance. • When looking at the curves in Figure 3 , we can find that: 1) across all the settings, accepted length is approximately unimodal with respect to the draft temperature, making it easier to tune; 2) the curves are quite flat when T d T_{d} is near the optimal choice, implying that the current draft temperature grid should be sufficient for evaluating temperature scaling; 3) the trend of the curves for different tasks are relatively consistent for the same draft model, implying consistency in the distribution gap observed in Section 4 across domains, though the curves for different models may be more different. • We can observe that temperature scaling improves the average accepted length by approximately 5-10%, e.g., from 5.275 5.275 to 5.773 5.773 for Qwen3.6-35B-A3B with DFlash, when employing the same draft temperature across tasks for each model pair, the improvement consistently exists across different tasks. For DSpark, there is also a 3%-9% gain in average accepted length, with a generally larger T d T_{d} . Subsequent work improves draft efficiency and alignment through alternative backbones and distillation ( Choi et al., 2025 ; Zhou et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ) , and expands candidate coverage through tree-based verification ( Miao et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2024b ; Li et al., 2026b ) . Medusa, EAGLE, and related draft-head designs introduce additional decoding heads or a lightweight draft layer conditioned on target features instead of standalone draft models ( Cai et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2024c ; Ankner et al., 2024 ) , and the latter state-of-the-art methods follow this design, including self-speculation methods ( Zhang et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2024 ) and EAGLE-3 ( Li et al., 2025 ) . ParallelSpec, P-EAGLE, DFlash, and related parallel drafters reduce sequential drafting overhead by predicting multiple positions in parallel, including through block-diffusion drafting ( Xiao et al., 2024 ; Hui et al., 2026 ; An et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2026 ) . Built upon the parallelism idea, DSpark augments a parallel backbone with lightweight autoregressive correction and confidence-based verification scheduling ( Cheng et al., 2026 ) . Confidence calibration. Confidence calibration aligns predicted confidence with empirical correctness and has been studied through post-hoc maps and calibration-aware training ( Guo et al., 2017 ; Kumar et al., 2018 ; Mukhoti et al., 2020 ; Wang, 2023 ) . Post-hoc approaches include binning, parametric scaling, and their compositions ( Naeini et al., 2015 ; Kull et al., 2017 ; Kull et al., 2019 ; Kumar et al., 2019 ; Zhang et al., 2020 ; Ding et al., 2021 ) . More recent studies also examine token-adaptive temperature scaling for language models ( Desai and Durrett, 2020 ; Xie et al., 2024 ) . Post-hoc draft calibration in speculative decoding. Draft calibration is largely unexplored in the literature, and prior works with temperature and distribution adjustment address several distinct objectives ( Wang et al., 2025 ; Ouyang et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ; Berdoz et al., 2026 ; Zhou et al., 2026 ) , with the following works as examples. SubSpec sharpens draft probabilities to improve cumulative-probability ranking in deep draft trees for offloaded inference with a greedy target, but does not systematically study the draft calibration ( Wang et al., 2025 ) . Ouyang et al. (2024) study the interaction between the training data of the draft model and decoding temperatures, but does not consider differentiating the temperature of the draft model. Other work calibrates confidence for control decisions: SpecBound temperature-scales shallow-layer outputs for early exit, while DSpark calibrates predicted prefix acceptance for verification scheduling ( Wen and Feng, 2026 ; Cheng et al., 2026 ) . Differently, we focus on systematically studying the distribution gap between draft and target models and methods to mitigate the gap. 4 Underconfident Draft Models We start from examining the current popular open-source draft models’ distribution gap compared to the corresponding target models, which forms the basis of applying post-hoc draft calibration methods. While Guo et al. (2017) discovers that modern neural networks tend to be overconfident in the choice they make, we find that draft models are generally underconfident compared to target models, admitting a consistently lower probability for top candidates. In other words, the draft distribution is generally flatter. 4.1 Experiment Settings & Metrics Unless otherwise specified, we employ the following experiment settings for speculative decoding evaluation throughout the paper. We evaluate nine target–draft pairs using community open-source EAGLE-3 ( Li et al., 2025 ) , DFlash ( Chen et al., 2026 ) , and DSpark ( Cheng et al., 2026 ) checkpoints for our evaluation. Target Models include GPT-OSS-120B, Gemma-4-31B-IT, and the Qwen series. Table 5 lists the exact pairings, checkpoint links, and chain lengths, which we generally follow the recommended settings. We use eight benchmarks spanning math (GSM8K, MATH-500, AIME 2025), code (HumanEval, MBPP, LiveCodeBench), and chat (MT-Bench, Arena-Hard v2), with sources and citations listed in Table 6 . We use low-reasoning/no-thinking chat template in the experiments unless otherwise specified. The experiments are done on SpecForge ( Li et al., 2026a ) /SGLang ( Zheng et al., 2024 ) stack with independent draft-temperature control and use chain proposals and rejection sampling with the calibrated draft probabilities. The temperature for the target model is fixed at T t = 1 T_{t}=1 , and generation is capped at 2,048 tokens. Each model pair keeps its chain length fixed across calibration methods. Please refer to more evaluation details in Appendix A . We use the accepted length as our evaluation metric: output tokens committed per verification round, including the bonus token. We aggregate rounds within each task and report an equal-weight mean across tasks. Distribution diagnostics average over eligible draft positions, where all preceding proposals in the block were accepted. 4.2 Draft Models can learn top candidates well, but are underconfident We use the same inference setup for draft and target models as default in this section. Generally consistent top candidates. We start from examining how consistent the top candidates learned by the draft model are with the target model. In Figure 1 , we show the overlap percentage between the top-k candidates of draft and target distributions regardless of order, i.e., how many of the top-k candidates are the same between target and draft models. We can observe that the draft model can learn around 70% or more for the top-1 token, showing its capability for catching the top candidate in the target distribution. The correctness tends to decrease, but it still remains more than 40% up to the top 16 candidates. Figure 1: The overlap percentage of top-k candidates in target and draft distributions on three different draft models, where k = 1 , 2 , 4 , 8 , 16 k=1,2,4,8,16 . Underconfident draft model. While the top candidates are generally learned correctly, we observe a consistent gap between the draft and target distributions. Figure 2 shows the probability draft and target distributions give the top-1 candidate when they agree, and the entropy of the distributions. Across different tasks and state-of-the-art speculative decoding algorithms, there exists a consistent gap between the top-1 probability of draft and target distributions, even if the draft model predicts it correctly – the draft model is underconfident about its top candidate choice compared to the target distribution. The consistently higher entropy also provides further evidence that the draft distribution is generally flatter than the target distribution. To conclude, the draft models are overall underconfident compared to the target model. Remark 1 (Why this distribution gap exists) . This consistent distribution gap is actually surprising since the draft distribution should be trained to match the target distribution. We hypothesize that this may be related to the limited capacity of draft models, making it hard to learn a sharp distribution as the target model. The settings of the training recipe could also be a potential reason for this. As discussed in Section 5.1 , DeepSeek-trained draft models have a smaller draft-target distribution gap across different speculative decoding algorithms. For example, the KL loss employed by the standard draft model training pipeline may also contribute to this, since it biases from the ℓ 1 \ell_{1} distribution gap ( Samarin et al., 2026 ) . items.summary: Today, the European Commission and eight Member States are launching the European Digital Infrastructure Consortium on Education (EDU-EDIC) to pool resources and develop shared, secure and interoperable digital infrastructure and services for education. GettyImages © anyaberkut The new consortium on education brings together Belgium, Croatia, Finland, France, Greece, Slovenia, Spain and the Netherlands, which will be hosting the EDIC. The initiative will strengthen Europe's technological resilience while making high-quality digital tools accessible to schools, teachers and learners. It will also help narrow the digital divide in education by supporting solutions that can be used across national education systems, regardless of their resources or technological capacity. Today's launch marks an important milestone in fostering innovation and excellence in education and contributing to the EU's technological sovereignty ambitions. Executive Vice-Presidents Henna Virkkunen and Roxana Mînzatu, together with Judith Tielen, Minister for Primary and Secondary Education of the Netherlands, will welcome the launch. Henna Virkkunen, Executive Vice-President for Tech Sovereignty, Security and Democracy, said: “Today's launch of the European Digital Infrastructure Consortium on Education is an important step towards achieving Europe's technological sovereignty in one of our most sensitive and strategic sectors. Education shapes our future, and Europe must be able to rely on trusted, safe and interoperable digital solutions that reflect European values and principles. By working together with the Member States, we can build a resilient European digital education infrastructure that supports learners, educators and schools across the Union.” Roxana Mînzatu, Executive Vice-President for Social Rights and Skills, Quality Jobs and Preparedness, said: “Recently, we officially launched the Education and Skills Package and announced the establishment of the EDU-EDIC consortium. Today, we are reiterating our commitment to reinforce education for Europe's future. Our priority is to ensure that education is ready for the AI era. We will work together with Member States to pool expertise in strategic areas such as cloud infrastructure, AI for education, secure data exchange across educational institutions, and Europe's education technology (EdTech) sector.” You can also read more about other European Digital Infrastructure Consortium (EDIC) . Related content News article 20 November 2026 Member States join forces to develop sovereign digital infrastructure on education Eight EU countries join forces to develop trusted, accessible digital education services and strengthen digital sovereignty. Last update 24 November 2026 Print as PDF

items.content: The second meeting of the AI Act Advisory Forum took place, in hybrid format, on Monday 16 November in Brussels. ©AdobeStock Nataliya One of the highlights of the meeting was the election of the two co-Chairs. Mrs Laura Lázaro Cabrera and Mrs Catarina Nunes Santos were elected. Both co-Chairs have taken on the responsibility of leading the Forum and representing its views for the next two years. Mrs Laura Lázaro Cabrera, representing the non-commercial views of the Forum, is Director of the Equity and Data programme and Deputy Director and Counsel to the Center for Democracy and Technology (CDT) Europe in Brussels, where she leads the work promoting the effective protection of fundamental human rights in the implementation of European Union legislation regulating new technologies. Mrs Catarina Santos Nunes, representing the commercial views of the Forum, is the Chief Operating Officer and Chief Compliance Office at Starkdata. Starkdata is a Portuguese company and provides an AI-powered predictive analytics platform which enables businesses to make data-driven decisions. Forum members adopted the Forum's Rule of Procedure, giving the Forum a clear framework for its functioning and for its decision-making process. Items discussed The meeting was kicked off with presentations from the AI Office. Updates on the current work of the AI Office were shared, and included insights on its enforcement activities, its work on innovation, the EU KIDS Act, and the Action Plan on Cybersecurity and AI. Discussions on the stocktaking on technological developments of AI, covering the latest developments in terms of AI capabilities, incidents as well as industrial application and AI R&D automation, also took place. The Chair of the AI Board , Mrs Jean Carberry, the Chair and the Vice-Chair of the Scientific Panel , Mr Seán Ó hÉigeartaigh, and Nicolas Moës, gave Advisory Forum participants information on their two respective bodies, exploring the synergies between the Advisory Forum, the AI Board and the Scientific Panel, the governance bodies established under the EU AI Act. The Advisory Forum was presented with possible work streams on which the AI Office wishes to seek its advice. Members were invited to discuss one of two topics: AI companions or AI agents, as well as the future of its work. The discussions took place in breakout groups, which subsequently reported to the plenary, sharing their main conclusions on both topics. Last update 24 November 2026 Print as PDF

items.content: Building on the solid foundation of the EU-Kenya strategic partnership and the launch of the EU-Kenya Digital Dialogue on 18 March 2026 in Nairobi, the European Commission and the Government of Kenya met for the next EU-Kenya Digital Dialogue. © European Commission Topics such as digital networks and infrastructure, AI, data adequacy, digital identity and online safety were jointly discussed. The EU-Kenya Digital Dialogue took place in Brussels on 23-24 November 2026. Both sides reaffirmed their strong commitment to work closely in joint areas and launched a roadmap to strengthen cooperation in the digital domain. EU and Kenya advance on strategic digital infrastructure investments At present the Team Europe investment pipeline is set to expand aerial fibre, bringing internet to 3,000 schools, health centres and digital hubs. Both sides spoke more widely on the rollout of secure, trusted digital networks and infrastructure, including submarine cable projects, satellite connectivity, fibre optics, sovereign data centres and cloud infrastructures. Kenya and EU connect AI ecosystems through AI Factories The EU and Kenya agreed to deepen the links between their AI ecosystems through EU-Kenya AI Factories partnerships, focusing on use cases such as language diversity and agriculture. They also agreed to explore an EU-Kenya advanced AI talent partnership, and an open-access AI compute facility, to bring compute capacity to Kenyan startups, small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and research institutes. EU and Kenya positively conclude technical adequacy negotiations and move towards adoption Kenya and the EU took an important step forward in their strategic partnership by positively concluding the technical adequacy negotiations. Both parties will now initiate the respective formal processes for the adoption of adequacy decisions. Once adopted, the mutual adequacy arrangement would facilitate trusted cross-border transfers of personal data between Kenya and the European Union. Kenya and EU make progress on Digital Public Infrastructure and Digital Identity cooperation Both sides agreed to strengthen technical work on Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI), including trusted digital identity and interoperability under the EU Digital Identity Framework, including the EU Digital Identity Wallet and trust services. Building on Kenya’s DPI Roadmap, the partnership will explore the development of specific DPI use cases to strengthen whole-of-government integration, improve digital public service delivery and promote secure, inclusive and citizen-centred digital transformation. EU and Kenya strengthen collaboration on online safety Both sides also agreed to intensify technical exchanges on online safety and platform governance, in particular on the protection of minors online. Additionally, EU Digital SME Alliance and the Digital transformation Centre Kenya launched a B2B matchmaking partnership . This will foster commercial partnerships between SMEs on both sides, creating jobs and expanding opportunities. Background On 18 March 2026, the EU and Kenya launched the EU–Kenya Digital Dialogue . This was an important step in strengthening cooperation on digital policy and technological innovation. The dialogue focuses on shared priorities, including digital networks and infrastructures, artificial intelligence, eGovernance & Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI), data adequacy and online safety. You can read more information in the Joint Communiqué . Last update 24 November 2026 Print as PDF

items.content: Featured projects TL;DR With Torch-TensorRT 2.15 and ExecuTorch 1.6 you can compile a PyTorch model with TensorRT, save it as an ExecuTorch program, and run it from C++ or Python without loading torch. You stay in PyTorch the whole way, and whatever TensorRT can’t handle can still run on the GPU. On an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano it comes within 4% of the fastest TensorRT setup we measured, in both speed and memory. A 3.6-billion-parameter policy fits on the 8 GB board, where PyTorch eager mode runs out of memory. You compile with one pip install "torch_tensorrt[executorch]" . To run, the robot needs only ExecuTorch and a small TensorRT backend, not PyTorch. We talked about this work at PyTorch Conference 2026: Deploying Robot Policies Across Many Targets with ExecuTorch . https://pytorch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/et-trt.mp4 GR00T 1.7 (3B) on a Jetson Orin Nano 8GB: about 200 ms per action chunk. Why is it hard to run a PyTorch model with TensorRT on a robot? A robot runs its models on its own computer, like NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor or a custom board, and they have to finish on time. A policy, the model that decides what the robot does next, returns a short plan at a time, called an action chunk, say 50 actions. If the next chunk isn’t ready when the robot finishes the current one, the robot stops and waits. And everything shares the same memory: the CPU, the GPU, the cameras and every model. Offloading to a server adds a network round trip, which can easily take 100 ms, over a link the robot can’t always count on. On NVIDIA hardware the fastest way to run a model is TensorRT , NVIDIA’s inference compiler. Until now, getting a PyTorch model into TensorRT meant one of four things: Go through ONNX. We call this ONNX-TensorRT in the tables. Export the model to an ONNX file and build a TensorRT engine from it. It’s fast and well proven, but your model has to get through two converters you don’t own: PyTorch’s ONNX exporter and TensorRT’s ONNX parser. If either one doesn’t know an op, the build fails, and the usual way out is writing a TensorRT plugin in C++. Write it by hand. Rebuild the model layer by layer with TensorRT’s network definition API . tensorrtx does this for many popular models, and early TensorRT-LLM did it for language models. You get full control, but every new model is new work, and checking the result against PyTorch is on you. Use TensorRT Model Connect. NVIDIA’s TensorRT Model Connect , in public preview, builds TensorRT engines straight from supported Hugging Face checkpoints, with no ONNX step, and runs them from C++ without PyTorch. It covers the models on its supported list. Use Torch-TensorRT inside PyTorch. Torch-TensorRT converts PyTorch ops to TensorRT directly, no ONNX file involved. But what it normally produces, an ExportedProgram or an AOTInductor .pt2 package, needs libtorch to run. That’s more than 1 GB of libraries, and a process that loads it holds hundreds of MB that inference never uses. The ONNX route and the ExecuTorch route. Today we’re adding a new way: Torch-TensorRT 2.15 compiles the model with TensorRT and saves it as an ExecuTorch 1.6 program that runs without libtorch. It skips ONNX and captures the model with PyTorch’s own torch.export . If TensorRT can’t convert part of the model, preprocessing included, you can send that part to ExecuTorch’s CUDA backend, which runs it on the GPU in the same program on the same CUDA stream instead of failing the build. The TensorRT parts are ordinary TensorRT engines, so the model runs about as fast as it does when you call TensorRT directly. How it works ExecuTorch is PyTorch’s solution for running models on edge devices. You compile a model ahead of time into a program, and a small runtime runs it without libtorch, from C++ or Python. Hardware support comes from backends : besides TensorRT there are CUDA , Intel OpenVINO , Qualcomm QNN , Apple Core ML and MLX , Arm , Vulkan , and XNNPACK for CPUs. Torch-TensorRT could already save ExecuTorch programs with output_format="executorch" . What’s new in Torch-TensorRT 2.15 and ExecuTorch 1.6 is that the workflow is production ready: one install, prebuilt C++ libraries, a Python runtime that doesn’t need PyTorch, and a few features for small boards. We call it ExecuTorch-TensorRT. Take a toy model that needs two backends: class Toy(torch.nn.Module): def forward(self, x): return torch.cos(torch.erfinv(torch.tanh(x))) The toy model, split across two backends. Capture and split. torch.export turns the model into a graph of PyTorch ops. TensorRT claims every part it can convert. It has no converter for erfinv , so the ExecuTorch CUDA backend takes that part instead. The compiler tells you which ops didn’t go to TensorRT, and why. Compile and pack. TensorRT builds an engine for each part it claimed, and the CUDA backend compiles its part with AOTInductor. The engines go into a .pte file, and the CUDA backend’s weights go into a .ptd data file next to it. Load and run. On the robot, the ExecuTorch runtime hands each part to its backend. Inputs, outputs and the tensors passed between the two backends can stay on the GPU, with no round trip through the CPU. If you set use_cuda_graphs=True , each engine’s GPU work is recorded once as a CUDA graph and replayed with a single launch, which makes every call cheaper. If your model has a custom op that neither TensorRT nor the CUDA backend can compile, you still don’t need a TensorRT plugin in C++. Write the op as a Triton kernel and register it with torch.library.triton_op . The CUDA backend compiles it into the program like any other part of the model, and the robot runs it without Triton or PyTorch installed. ExecuTorch’s own CUDA kernels for attention, mixture-of-experts layers and 4-bit matmuls are written this way. Getting started Install pip install "torch_tensorrt[executorch]" That gets you PyTorch, Torch-TensorRT, ExecuTorch and a small TensorRT backend for ExecuTorch. You need PyTorch only to compile. The compiled program runs without it; see Run, in Python, without torch for the smaller install for the robot. The wheels are built for CUDA 13.2 on Linux, x86-64 and Arm64, which on an NVIDIA Jetson means JetPack 7.2 or newer. On Arm64 the first install also pulls about 2.6 GB of TensorRT libraries from NVIDIA, so give it a few minutes. It can’t reuse the TensorRT that ships with NVIDIA JetPack, because Torch-TensorRT 2.15 needs TensorRT 11.4 and JetPack 7.2 comes with TensorRT 10. Export, in Python import torch import torch_tensorrt from executorch.backends.cuda.cuda_backend import CudaBackend from executorch.backends.cuda.cuda_partitioner import CudaPartitioner with torch.no_grad(): model = MyPolicy().eval().cuda() example = (torch.randn(1, 3, 224, 224, device="cuda"),) exported = torch.export.export(model, example) trt_model = torch_tensorrt.dynamo.compile( exported, arg_inputs=example, min_block_size=1, truncate_double=True ) torch_tensorrt.save( trt_model, "policy.pte", output_format="executorch", # Everything TensorRT does not take goes to the CUDA backend. partitioners=[CudaPartitioner([CudaBackend.generate_method_name_compile_spec("forward")])], ) The CUDA backend needs a CUDA toolkit (nvcc) at export time, and it writes aoti_cuda_blob.ptd next to the .pte. Give each export its own folder and ship both files. Memory: median of three runs, over the last 30 s of 120 s; files the process only reads, such as the program files, are not counted, and a range means the runs differed by more than 5%. The TensorRT columns and torch.compile replay CUDA graphs . Maximum power, GPU clock locked. Bold is best in the row. Differences of a few milliseconds are within run-to-run noise. Measured with the released Torch-TensorRT 2.15.0 and ExecuTorch 1.6.0. Benchmark method and full tables . A few things stand out: On the Orin Nano, ExecuTorch-TensorRT is within 4% of ONNX-TensorRT on every policy, and up to 6.4x faster than PyTorch eager mode. Memory is about the same as ONNX-TensorRT, and lower on the two small policies. The Torch-TensorRT column runs the same TensorRT engines inside PyTorch. On an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor developer kit, the high-end robot board, resource limits are less of an issue, but memory efficiency still lets more workloads fit on the device. Again, the compiled paths end up with similar performance. On a green context TensorRT warns about that, and an engine that uses kernels needing more SMs than the context has can fail, so give each green context enough SMs for its engine. You can follow which policies export and run on each GPU in this tracking issue , which uses newer builds than the tables above. You stay in PyTorch the whole way, and whatever TensorRT can’t handle can still run on the GPU. On an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano it comes within 4% of the fastest TensorRT setup we measured, in both speed and memory. A 3.6-billion-parameter policy fits on the 8 GB board, where PyTorch eager mode runs out of memory. You compile with one pip install "torch_tensorrt[executorch]" . To run, the robot needs only ExecuTorch and a small TensorRT backend, not PyTorch. We talked about this work at PyTorch Conference 2026: Deploying Robot Policies Across Many Targets with ExecuTorch . https://pytorch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/et-trt.mp4 GR00T 1.7 (3B) on a Jetson Orin Nano 8GB: about 200 ms per action chunk. Why is it hard to run a PyTorch model with TensorRT on a robot? A robot runs its models on its own computer, like NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor or a custom board, and they have to finish on time. A policy, the model that decides what the robot does next, returns a short plan at a time, called an action chunk, say 50 actions. If the next chunk isn’t ready when the robot finishes the current one, the robot stops and waits. And everything shares the same memory: the CPU, the GPU, the cameras and every model. Offloading to a server adds a network round trip, which can easily take 100 ms, over a link the robot can’t always count on. On NVIDIA hardware the fastest way to run a model is TensorRT , NVIDIA’s inference compiler. Until now, getting a PyTorch model into TensorRT meant one of four things: Go through ONNX. We call this ONNX-TensorRT in the tables. Export the model to an ONNX file and build a TensorRT engine from it. It’s fast and well proven, but your model has to get through two converters you don’t own: PyTorch’s ONNX exporter and TensorRT’s ONNX parser. If either one doesn’t know an op, the build fails, and the usual way out is writing a TensorRT plugin in C++. Write it by hand. Rebuild the model layer by layer with TensorRT’s network definition API . tensorrtx does this for many popular models, and early TensorRT-LLM did it for language models. You get full control, but every new model is new work, and checking the result against PyTorch is on you. Use TensorRT Model Connect. NVIDIA’s TensorRT Model Connect , in public preview, builds TensorRT engines straight from supported Hugging Face checkpoints, with no ONNX step, and runs them from C++ without PyTorch. It covers the models on its supported list. Use Torch-TensorRT inside PyTorch. Torch-TensorRT converts PyTorch ops to TensorRT directly, no ONNX file involved. But what it normally produces, an ExportedProgram or an AOTInductor .pt2 package, needs libtorch to run. That’s more than 1 GB of libraries, and a process that loads it holds hundreds of MB that inference never uses. The ONNX route and the ExecuTorch route. Today we’re adding a new way: Torch-TensorRT 2.15 compiles the model with TensorRT and saves it as an ExecuTorch 1.6 program that runs without libtorch. It skips ONNX and captures the model with PyTorch’s own torch.export . If TensorRT can’t convert part of the model, preprocessing included, you can send that part to ExecuTorch’s CUDA backend, which runs it on the GPU in the same program on the same CUDA stream instead of failing the build. The TensorRT parts are ordinary TensorRT engines, so the model runs about as fast as it does when you call TensorRT directly. How it works ExecuTorch is PyTorch’s solution for running models on edge devices. You compile a model ahead of time into a program, and a small runtime runs it without libtorch, from C++ or Python. Hardware support comes from backends : besides TensorRT there are CUDA , Intel OpenVINO , Qualcomm QNN , Apple Core ML and MLX , Arm , Vulkan , and XNNPACK for CPUs. Torch-TensorRT could already save ExecuTorch programs with output_format="executorch" . We call it ExecuTorch-TensorRT. Take a toy model that needs two backends: class Toy(torch.nn.Module): def forward(self, x): return torch.cos(torch.erfinv(torch.tanh(x))) The toy model, split across two backends. Capture and split. torch.export turns the model into a graph of PyTorch ops. TensorRT claims every part it can convert. It has no converter for erfinv , so the ExecuTorch CUDA backend takes that part instead. The compiler tells you which ops didn’t go to TensorRT, and why. Compile and pack. TensorRT builds an engine for each part it claimed, and the CUDA backend compiles its part with AOTInductor. The engines go into a .pte file, and the CUDA backend’s weights go into a .ptd data file next to it. Load and run. On the robot, the ExecuTorch runtime hands each part to its backend. Inputs, outputs and the tensors passed between the two backends can stay on the GPU, with no round trip through the CPU. items.content: Trustworthy AI / Cybersecurity English 한국어 中文 Inside NVIDIA Sentry: Secure AI Agents at Runtime NVIDIA Sentry governs agent access requests, monitors runtime activity, and contains threats from an isolated hardware security layer in milliseconds. Oct 21, 2026 By Ofir Arkin , Ariel Kit and Itay Ozery Like Discuss (0) L T F R E AI-Generated Summary NVIDIA Sentry monitors AI agents and enforces access policies from a hardware-isolated trust domain on BlueField-4 DPUs, independent of host software. DOCA Tower acts as a transparent proxy that terminates TLS and evaluates agent requests against Open Policy Agent rules, while DOCA Argus provides real-time memory introspection of the agent's execution environment. The framework correlates network traffic with runtime context to enforce policies based on container hashes, process integrity, and approved software bills of materials. Specialized AI models classify agent communications inline or out of band to detect behavioral drift, and in-silicon enforcement can contain agents within milliseconds. Attested telemetry and tamper-evident records preserved on BlueField-4 support forensic investigation and integration with enterprise security platforms. Next Steps Explore NVIDIA DOCA libraries and microservices to experiment with out-of-band observability and infrastructure enforcement. Powered by NVIDIA Nemotron. AI-generated content may summarize information incompletely. Verify important information. Learn more An AI agent can complete its assignment and still cross a security boundary. Recent incidents show that agents can circumvent security controls while using tools, credentials, and services to pursue their assigned goals. Monitoring and enforcement need to operate outside the agent’s reach so that it can’t alter or disable them. NVIDIA Sentry is a security software framework that monitors AI agents and enforces policies governing their access to models, tools, and data. Part of the NVIDIA OpenShell reference architecture announced at GTC Berlin, it’s built on NVIDIA DOCA , runs on NVIDIA BlueField-4 DPUs , and provides host-isolated runtime protection for AI agents. NVIDIA Sentry validates that an agent operates according to its designed intent and within its defined operational boundaries. Trusted even when host resources can’t be trusted, it controls the agent’s only path to the model, providing tamper-evident traceability of agent activity while enforcing granular security controls on agent access in silicon. In addition to inspecting agent communications, NVIDIA Sentry uses out-of-band observability to establish real-time situational awareness, continuously evaluating agents’ runtime security and behavior to validate their security and integrity. This post explains how NVIDIA Sentry evaluates agent requests, detects threats, and enforces security policies independently of host software. An independent security layer for agent runtime protection An earlier agentic AI security post described how NVIDIA BlueField runs security services in a hardware trust domain independent from the host. NVIDIA Sentry builds on that foundation to continuously monitor AI agent behavior and enforce access policies independently of host software, establishing a strict security boundary in a separate hardware trust domain outside the agent’s reach to keep agents operating within their designed intent. Software runtime boundaries remain essential. NVIDIA OpenShell is a secure runtime for autonomous agents that governs what an agent can do. OpenShell separates policy enforcement from the agent workload, so a compromised agent can’t change its own restrictions. NVIDIA Sentry adds an independent hardware safeguard out of band, running on BlueField-4, beyond the agent’s reach and knowledge. In the OpenShell reference architecture, agents execute on NVIDIA Vera CPUs , while BlueField-4 sits on the node’s only path to the model. NVIDIA Sentry inspects agent-to-model communications and enforces access policies without relying on the agent to report its own behavior. Memory introspection adds context about the agent’s execution environment, such as a container or microVM, to help detect external threats and agent misbehavior. Governing agent communications DOCA Tower is NVIDIA Sentry’s AI security gateway. Built on Envoy , the open source edge and service proxy, it operates as a transparent proxy for agent traffic, placing a bidirectional inspection layer between an agent and the external environment. Agent network traffic reaches BlueField-4 through a direct network I/O path that bypasses host OS/hypervisor packet processing. All of the agent’s network communications are governed by NVIDIA Sentry as BlueField-4 sits on the only path to the model and to the outside world. An agent’s network access boundary is controlled using DOCA Flow and DOCA Tower, which work in concert to restrict agent access to approved resources. DOCA Flow is used to implement a layer-4 firewall for each agent, accelerated in silicon on BlueField-4. The firewall blocks connections to unauthorized destinations and forwards permitted traffic to DOCA Tower for layer-7 (application layer) inspection, authorization, and additional security checks. DOCA Tower acts as a transparent proxy, performing Transport Layer Security (TLS) termination using built-in, in-silicon TLS acceleration. For connections configured for inspection, it decrypts the agent traffic permitted by the layer-4 firewall to inspect and control agent communications. NVIDIA Sentry uses the Open Policy Agent (OPA), an open source policy engine, to evaluate access requests against defined policies. OPA uses Rego, a declarative domain-specific language designed to evaluate complex hierarchical data structures. OPA runs locally in memory and can evaluate requests in under a millisecond, depending on policy complexity and configuration. DOCA Tower is compatible with OpenShell policies, using OPA to extend network access policies and runtime controls into BlueField-4 and to the infrastructure. Figure 1. NVIDIA Sentry uses DOCA Tower to inspect access requests and a policy engine to evaluate authorization, with runtime context from DOCA Argus Enforcing agent access policies with runtime context An agent’s network communications provide only part of the information needed to assess its security and integrity. Visibility into the agent’s execution environment adds context for evaluating access requests that go beyond a traditional resource access policy. DOCA Argus provides real-time visibility into an agent’s execution environment and operational state, giving NVIDIA Sentry additional context about agent access requests. It uses live memory introspection to analyze selected regions of volatile host memory and obtain independent evidence of the system’s operational state. DOCA Argus runs independently of the host, analyzing host memory on BlueField-4 without host-resident agents. This agentless design provides independent runtime visibility while preserving host compute resources. By operating outside the host in its own isolated trust domain, DOCA Argus remains beyond the reach of host software even if the host is compromised. DOCA Argus maps the execution environment in real time—for example, containers to their respective pods and sandboxes to microVMs—and identifies the running processes and their properties within each environment. It also maps relationships between processes and threads, file access, network connections, loaded libraries, CPUs, GPUs, memory, and other system resources. DOCA Argus tracks containers, processes, and loaded libraries using their associated hashes. This runtime context enables NVIDIA Sentry to connect agent access requests to the processes and execution environments behind them, enforcing policies that consider both the requested action and the security and integrity of the agent making it. Using runtime context to evaluate agent access NVIDIA Sentry correlates network connection information from DOCA Tower with runtime context from DOCA Argus to evaluate access requests. NVIDIA Sentry uses this context to enforce policies based on additional attributes and assertions provided by DOCA Argus. It also enriches tamper-evident records of agent activity with runtime context, reducing the need for downstream correlation. Figure 1 shows how these checks work. DOCA Tower uses its policy engine to correlate a network connection with the agent’s process that initiated it, its properties, and the container it belongs to. A network access policy can, for example, require that the container’s hash match a list of approved container hashes. It can also require that the initiating process, identified by its hash, appear in the container software bill of materials (SBOM), have permission to initiate network connections, and use an approved execution path and command-line arguments. DOCA Tower then checks whether policy permits the requested access—for example, access to an API and permission to perform the requested action. NVIDIA Sentry uses DOCA Argus real-time observations and alerts to continuously evaluate agent security. Potential warning signs include executing unapproved tools; using ptrace to attack another process or spawn a process that attacks the agent; excessive outbound traffic suggesting data leakage; unauthorized file access or changes; CPU spikes; excessive writes to temporary folders; and large-scale file deletion. When NVIDIA Sentry detects any deviation, it can request millisecond-scale in-silicon containment. Extending controls to agent interactions Agent security policies need to govern both what leaves the sandbox and what comes back. Requests can expose sensitive information or initiate unauthorized operations. Responses can introduce malicious instructions or other content that redirects an agent from its assigned goals. NVIDIA Sentry uses DOCA Tower’s extensible inspection capabilities to apply controls to requests and responses. These controls can: Apply IP-, URL-, and protocol-level restrictions to agent communications. Capture tamper-evident records of agent requests, responses, and data flows for behavioral analysis and investigation. Govern agent-to-agent (A2A) and Model Context Protocol (MCP) traffic. Detect and redact personally identifiable information and secrets, including API keys, tokens, and passwords. Identify and block content prohibited by policy. NVIDIA Sentry evaluates inspected requests and responses throughout an agent’s session, applying policy as the agent accesses models, tools, APIs, and services. Evaluating agent behavior using specialized models NVIDIA Sentry integrates with specialized AI models to analyze agent communications and classify agent behavior using tool calls and available reasoning traces. These models run locally or remotely on dedicated GPU-accelerated systems. The classifiers assess whether an agent’s behavior remains consistent with an agent’s designed intent or indicates behavioral drift. The models can classify agent communications inline or out of band. Inline classification can trigger blocking before potentially harmful content reaches its destination. Out-of-band classification can trigger a response action after detecting agent misbehavior. Tamper-evident activity records and detection results provide forensic evidence for further incident investigations. Agent communications require continuous classification to detect misbehavior. DOCA Argus complements this classification with ongoing analysis of the agent’s operational environment to evaluate runtime security and behavior. Figure 2. NVIDIA Sentry uses DOCA Tower to submit inspected communications to a specialized model for classification, where potentially harmful content is blocked inline NVIDIA Sentry can contain and quarantine agents within milliseconds using BlueField-4 in-silicon enforcement capabilities without the cooperation of the agent or the host software. These independent controls matter when software boundaries fail. Even if an agent escapes its sandbox, NVIDIA Sentry retains its monitoring and enforcement capabilities as it operates from BlueField-4’s isolated trust domain. Enterprise security platforms can also use NVIDIA Sentry telemetry to correlate detections and request response actions. The protected record preserves the observed activity and policy context that led to enforcement for subsequent review. Figure 3. NVIDIA Sentry combines interaction telemetry, runtime detections, and policy context with enterprise security integrations to drive response actions through DOCA Tower Using agent identity in access decisions Security controls must connect an agent’s identity with its permissions and requested action. NVIDIA Sentry uses this identity context in application-layer policy evaluation. DOCA Tower integrates with SPIFFE/SPIRE to support verifiable workload identity and supports integration with partner identity systems. Identity establishes who is making a request. Authorization policies determine which resources an identity may access and which operations are permitted. Runtime evidence adds context about the execution environment associated with the request. This approach connects identity and runtime security. If an agent’s behavior or integrity changes, NVIDIA Sentry can use that context when evaluating subsequent access requests, applying the organization’s defined policies. Preserving a trusted record of agent activity Security teams need evidence for incident investigations, even when an agent has escaped its sandbox or altered host-based logs. NVIDIA Sentry produces attested telemetry and tamper-evident records using BlueField-4’s independent trust domain. DOCA Tower records inspected communications and policy decisions outside the reach of the agent and host software, while DOCA Argus contributes independently observed runtime signals. An agent that changes a log inside its own environment cannot make the same change to the protected record maintained on BlueField-4. Attestation provides verifiable evidence of telemetry’s source and integrity. Security teams can use these records to reconstruct observed interactions, review enforcement decisions, and support audits. NVIDIA Sentry can supply this telemetry to enterprise security platforms, such as XDR and SIEM platforms and security data lakes, connecting agent activity with broader threat intelligence, detection logic, and incident-response workflows. Extending NVIDIA Sentry with enterprise security capabilities NVIDIA Sentry enables developers and cybersecurity providers to extend monitoring, governance, and enforcement through DOCA libraries and microservices. DOCA Tower uses Envoy’s extensibility, enabling partners to adapt existing plugins or develop new ones to run on BlueField. This provides a familiar foundation for integrating access controls, content inspection, telemetry, and specialized detection logic into the application-layer path. NVIDIA plans to publish core plugins to accelerate development, including a plugin that exposes agent communications for further analysis of available reasoning traces. Partners can combine these capabilities with their identity services, AI classifiers, threat intelligence, and security operations platforms. NVIDIA Sentry contributes independent runtime visibility and infrastructure enforcement, while connected platforms add enterprise context and coordinate investigation and response. Building layered protection for AI agents Scaling agentic AI requires continuous visibility into and control over what agents can access and do throughout execution. NVIDIA Sentry brings that control into an independent infrastructure domain, combining application-layer inspection through DOCA Tower with runtime evidence and visibility from DOCA Argus and in-silicon enforcement on BlueField-4. Alongside NVIDIA OpenShell, NVIDIA Sentry extends protection from software execution boundaries to a hardware-isolated safeguard. It enables security teams to evaluate agent identity, authority, interactions, and runtime integrity together—and act when behavior crosses defined boundaries. Developers and cybersecurity teams can begin exploring these foundations with NVIDIA DOCA . Available libraries and microservices, including DOCA Argus, DOCA Flow, and OVS-DOCA, provide a starting point for experimenting with out-of-band observability and infrastructure enforcement ahead of NVIDIA Sentry’s planned availability early next year.
