In the OpenShell reference architecture, agents execute on NVIDIA Vera CPUs , while BlueField-4 sits on the node’s only path to the model. NVIDIA Sentry inspects agent-to-model communications and enforces access policies without relying on the agent to report its own behavior. Memory introspection adds context about the agent’s execution environment, such as a container or microVM, to help detect external threats and agent misbehavior. Governing agent communications DOCA Tower is NVIDIA Sentry’s AI security gateway. Built on Envoy , the open source edge and service proxy, it operates as a transparent proxy for agent traffic, placing a bidirectional inspection layer between an agent and the external environment. Agent network traffic reaches BlueField-4 through a direct network I/O path that bypasses host OS/hypervisor packet processing. All of the agent’s network communications are governed by NVIDIA Sentry as BlueField-4 sits on the only path to the model and to the outside world. An agent’s network access boundary is controlled using DOCA Flow and DOCA Tower, which work in concert to restrict agent access to approved resources. DOCA Flow is used to implement a layer-4 firewall for each agent, accelerated in silicon on BlueField-4. The firewall blocks connections to unauthorized destinations and forwards permitted traffic to DOCA Tower for layer-7 (application layer) inspection, authorization, and additional security checks. DOCA Tower acts as a transparent proxy, performing Transport Layer Security (TLS) termination using built-in, in-silicon TLS acceleration. For connections configured for inspection, it decrypts the agent traffic permitted by the layer-4 firewall to inspect and control agent communications. NVIDIA Sentry uses the Open Policy Agent (OPA), an open source policy engine, to evaluate access requests against defined policies. OPA uses Rego, a declarative domain-specific language designed to evaluate complex hierarchical data structures. OPA runs locally in memory and can evaluate requests in under a millisecond, depending on policy complexity and configuration. DOCA Tower is compatible with OpenShell policies, using OPA to extend network access policies and runtime controls into BlueField-4 and to the infrastructure. Figure 1. NVIDIA Sentry uses DOCA Tower to inspect access requests and a policy engine to evaluate authorization, with runtime context from DOCA Argus Enforcing agent access policies with runtime context An agent’s network communications provide only part of the information needed to assess its security and integrity. Visibility into the agent’s execution environment adds context for evaluating access requests that go beyond a traditional resource access policy. DOCA Argus provides real-time visibility into an agent’s execution environment and operational state, giving NVIDIA Sentry additional context about agent access requests. It uses live memory introspection to analyze selected regions of volatile host memory and obtain independent evidence of the system’s operational state. DOCA Argus runs independently of the host, analyzing host memory on BlueField-4 without host-resident agents. This agentless design provides independent runtime visibility while preserving host compute resources. By operating outside the host in its own isolated trust domain, DOCA Argus remains beyond the reach of host software even if the host is compromised. DOCA Argus maps the execution environment in real time—for example, containers to their respective pods and sandboxes to microVMs—and identifies the running processes and their properties within each environment. It also maps relationships between processes and threads, file access, network connections, loaded libraries, CPUs, GPUs, memory, and other system resources. DOCA Argus tracks containers, processes, and loaded libraries using their associated hashes. This runtime context enables NVIDIA Sentry to connect agent access requests to the processes and execution environments behind them, enforcing policies that consider both the requested action and the security and integrity of the agent making it. Using runtime context to evaluate agent access NVIDIA Sentry correlates network connection information from DOCA Tower with runtime context from DOCA Argus to evaluate access requests. NVIDIA Sentry uses this context to enforce policies based on additional attributes and assertions provided by DOCA Argus. It also enriches tamper-evident records of agent activity with runtime context, reducing the need for downstream correlation. Figure 1 shows how these checks work. DOCA Tower uses its policy engine to correlate a network connection with the agent’s process that initiated it, its properties, and the container it belongs to. A network access policy can, for example, require that the container’s hash match a list of approved container hashes. It can also require that the initiating process, identified by its hash, appear in the container software bill of materials (SBOM), have permission to initiate network connections, and use an approved execution path and command-line arguments. DOCA Tower then checks whether policy permits the requested access—for example, access to an API and permission to perform the requested action. NVIDIA Sentry uses DOCA Argus real-time observations and alerts to continuously evaluate agent security. Potential warning signs include executing unapproved tools; using ptrace to attack another process or spawn a process that attacks the agent; excessive outbound traffic suggesting data leakage; unauthorized file access or changes; CPU spikes; excessive writes to temporary folders; and large-scale file deletion. When NVIDIA Sentry detects any deviation, it can request millisecond-scale in-silicon containment. Extending controls to agent interactions Agent security policies need to govern both what leaves the sandbox and what comes back. Requests can expose sensitive information or initiate unauthorized operations. Responses can introduce malicious instructions or other content that redirects an agent from its assigned goals. NVIDIA Sentry uses DOCA Tower’s extensible inspection capabilities to apply controls to requests and responses. These controls can: Apply IP-, URL-, and protocol-level restrictions to agent communications. Capture tamper-evident records of agent requests, responses, and data flows for behavioral analysis and investigation. Govern agent-to-agent (A2A) and Model Context Protocol (MCP) traffic. Detect and redact personally identifiable information and secrets, including API keys, tokens, and passwords. Identify and block content prohibited by policy. NVIDIA Sentry evaluates inspected requests and responses throughout an agent’s session, applying policy as the agent accesses models, tools, APIs, and services. Evaluating agent behavior using specialized models NVIDIA Sentry integrates with specialized AI models to analyze agent communications and classify agent behavior using tool calls and available reasoning traces. These models run locally or remotely on dedicated GPU-accelerated systems. The classifiers assess whether an agent’s behavior remains consistent with an agent’s designed intent or indicates behavioral drift. The models can classify agent communications inline or out of band. Inline classification can trigger blocking before potentially harmful content reaches its destination. Out-of-band classification can trigger a response action after detecting agent misbehavior. Tamper-evident activity records and detection results provide forensic evidence for further incident investigations. Agent communications require continuous classification to detect misbehavior. DOCA Argus complements this classification with ongoing analysis of the agent’s operational environment to evaluate runtime security and behavior. Figure 2. NVIDIA Sentry uses DOCA Tower to submit inspected communications to a specialized model for classification, where potentially harmful content is blocked inline NVIDIA Sentry can contain and quarantine agents within milliseconds using BlueField-4 in-silicon enforcement capabilities without the cooperation of the agent or the host software. These independent controls matter when software boundaries fail. Even if an agent escapes its sandbox, NVIDIA Sentry retains its monitoring and enforcement capabilities as it operates from BlueField-4’s isolated trust domain. Enterprise security platforms can also use NVIDIA Sentry telemetry to correlate detections and request response actions. The protected record preserves the observed activity and policy context that led to enforcement for subsequent review. Figure 3. NVIDIA Sentry combines interaction telemetry, runtime detections, and policy context with enterprise security integrations to drive response actions through DOCA Tower Using agent identity in access decisions Security controls must connect an agent’s identity with its permissions and requested action. NVIDIA Sentry uses this identity context in application-layer policy evaluation. DOCA Tower integrates with SPIFFE/SPIRE to support verifiable workload identity and supports integration with partner identity systems. Identity establishes who is making a request. Authorization policies determine which resources an identity may access and which operations are permitted. Runtime evidence adds context about the execution environment associated with the request. This approach connects identity and runtime security. If an agent’s behavior or integrity changes, NVIDIA Sentry can use that context when evaluating subsequent access requests, applying the organization’s defined policies. Preserving a trusted record of agent activity Security teams need evidence for incident investigations, even when an agent has escaped its sandbox or altered host-based logs. NVIDIA Sentry produces attested telemetry and tamper-evident records using BlueField-4’s independent trust domain. DOCA Tower records inspected communications and policy decisions outside the reach of the agent and host software, while DOCA Argus contributes independently observed runtime signals. An agent that changes a log inside its own environment cannot make the same change to the protected record maintained on BlueField-4. Attestation provides verifiable evidence of telemetry’s source and integrity. Security teams can use these records to reconstruct observed interactions, review enforcement decisions, and support audits. NVIDIA Sentry can supply this telemetry to enterprise security platforms, such as XDR and SIEM platforms and security data lakes, connecting agent activity with broader threat intelligence, detection logic, and incident-response workflows. Extending NVIDIA Sentry with enterprise security capabilities NVIDIA Sentry enables developers and cybersecurity providers to extend monitoring, governance, and enforcement through DOCA libraries and microservices. DOCA Tower uses Envoy’s extensibility, enabling partners to adapt existing plugins or develop new ones to run on BlueField. This provides a familiar foundation for integrating access controls, content inspection, telemetry, and specialized detection logic into the application-layer path. NVIDIA plans to publish core plugins to accelerate development, including a plugin that exposes agent communications for further analysis of available reasoning traces. Partners can combine these capabilities with their identity services, AI classifiers, threat intelligence, and security operations platforms. NVIDIA Sentry contributes independent runtime visibility and infrastructure enforcement, while connected platforms add enterprise context and coordinate investigation and response. Building layered protection for AI agents Scaling agentic AI requires continuous visibility into and control over what agents can access and do throughout execution. NVIDIA Sentry brings that control into an independent infrastructure domain, combining application-layer inspection through DOCA Tower with runtime evidence and visibility from DOCA Argus and in-silicon enforcement on BlueField-4. Alongside NVIDIA OpenShell, NVIDIA Sentry extends protection from software execution boundaries to a hardware-isolated safeguard. It enables security teams to evaluate agent identity, authority, interactions, and runtime integrity together—and act when behavior crosses defined boundaries. Developers and cybersecurity teams can begin exploring these foundations with NVIDIA DOCA . Available libraries and microservices, including DOCA Argus, DOCA Flow, and OVS-DOCA, provide a starting point for experimenting with out-of-band observability and infrastructure enforcement ahead of NVIDIA Sentry’s planned availability early next year. items.content: Simulation / Modeling / Design How to Run NVIDIA Cosmos 3 on Local AI Devices Using Hugging Face Diffusers Nov 24, 2026 By Atharva Joshi and Jibin Varghese Like Discuss (0) L T F R E AI-Generated Summary NVIDIA Cosmos 3 Nano is a world foundation model that generates videos from text, images, and other inputs to support physical AI development. The Cosmos-Framework offloading package enables running Cosmos 3 Nano on GPUs with as little as 12 GB of VRAM by storing model weights in system RAM and transferring them to the GPU as needed during generation. An FP8 checkpoint with native mixed precision reduces peak GPU memory usage while maintaining BF16 scaled dot-product attention for the attention layers. The adapter supports seven generation modalities including text-to-video, image-to-video, video-to-video, sound generation, action generation, and control-guided generation through the official Diffusers modular pipeline. Benchmark results across GeForce RTX 5070, 5080, 4090, and 5090 show pipeline latency and peak memory usage for each resolution and modality, with the RTX 5070 completing 720p text-to-video in 2,624.9 seconds at 9.94 GiB peak memory using BF16. Next Steps Download the Cosmos 3 Nano checkpoint and its FP8 branch on Hugging Face. Find examples and code in the Cosmos-Framework offloading package . Review the Diffusers memory optimization guide for CPU offloading and the Cosmos 3 pipeline documentation for supported generation workflows. Powered by NVIDIA Nemotron. AI-generated content may summarize information incompletely. Verify important information. Learn more Running video generation models locally can be challenging when model weights and intermediate data exceed available GPU memory. NVIDIA Cosmos 3 Nano is a world foundation model that generates videos from text, images, and other inputs to support physical AI development. Learn more about NVIDIA Cosmos for physical AI . This tutorial walks you through how to run Cosmos 3 Nano on a GPU with as little as 12 GB of VRAM by storing most model weights in system RAM and transferring them to the GPU as needed. Using Hugging Face Diffusers, you’ll generate your first video, explore sound and additional input types, and use an FP8 checkpoint to further reduce memory requirements. This streaming adapter builds on top of the native group offloading approach from the Hugging Face library to enable generation on a smaller GPU. The tradeoff is that this requires increased system RAM use and PCIe transfers for a smaller GPU-memory requirement. Note that this approach does not provide interactive latency or stream weights directly from disk during inference. Step 1: Generate your first video Use an existing Linux environment with Python 3.12 and a CUDA-enabled PyTorch build compatible with your GPU. The tested consumer-GPU hosts had approximately 128 GB of system RAM; this is not a measured minimum. Clone Cosmos-Framework and install its standalone offloading package in your active environment. Run all examples and benchmark commands below from the package directory: git clone https://github.com/NVIDIA/cosmos-framework.git cd cosmos-framework/packages/diffusers-cpu-offloading uv pip install '.[benchmarks]' Pass the Hugging Face repository ID directly to build_pipeline . The first load downloads the checkpoint. Subsequent loads reuse cached files. Safety checking is enabled by default. import torch from cosmos3_streaming import StreamingConfig, build_pipeline device = "cuda:0" config = StreamingConfig(device=device) pipe = build_pipeline( "nvidia/Cosmos3-Nano", config=config, dtype=torch.bfloat16, ) With no revision argument, the BF16 load uses the repository’s default branch. The default configuration chooses appropriate memory-saving behavior automatically. Start with BF16 and PyTorch scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) , the baseline used on all four tested GPUs. Set the video options This example generates 189 frames at 720p. For faster iteration on a 12 GB GPU, change height and width to 480 and 848, or 240 and 432. common_video_args = { "negative_prompt": "", "num_frames": 189, "height": 720, "width": 1280, "fps": 24.0, "num_inference_steps": 35, "guidance_scale": 6.0, "add_resolution_template": False, "add_duration_template": False, } Generate and save the video Next, generate and save the video using the following script: t2v = pipe( prompt='{"scene":"A robot arm working in a kitchen"}', generator=torch.Generator(device=device).manual_seed(123), output="videos", **common_video_args, ) # Save the returned video frames as an MP4 file: from diffusers.utils import export_to_video export_to_video(t2v, "cosmos3_t2v.mp4", fps=common_video_args["fps"]) Step 2: Offload weights storage The central idea is to store model weights in system RAM and use the GPU for computation. To run large models within tight VRAM limits, this execution model manages memory and compute across the CPU and GPU in four ways: Checkpoint weights that are not currently needed remain in system RAM, in BF16 or the checkpoint’s FP8 representation. The next transformer block is transferred to the GPU when required. Every matrix multiplication and attention operation runs on CUDA. The adapter manages memory for denoising, the variational autoencoder (VAE) that encodes and decodes video, and safety checking. With this approach, system RAM acts as the backing store for model weights. More demanding requests, including 720p Transfer on a 12 GB GPU, use an automatic lower-memory execution mode while keeping model computation on CUDA. Move weights from system RAM to the GPU Next, move weights from system RAM to the GPU. Figure 1 shows the path from checkpoint storage to GPU computation. Checkpoint files remain on disk between runs. During generation, system RAM is the backing store for weights that are not currently on the GPU. This is why a fast SSD helps with model loading, while sufficient system RAM and PCIe bandwidth matter during generation. Figure 1. Streaming model weights from system RAM to the GPU enables NVIDIA Cosmos 3 Nano generation without keeping the full model in GPU memory Reuse understanding context during generation Diffusers provides sequential, model-level, and group-level CPU offloading to move model components between CPU and GPU memory. The Cosmos adapter builds on those mechanisms and coordinates when the model’s understanding and generation pathways run. NVIDIA Cosmos 3 , an open omnimodal world foundation model for physical AI, has two complementary pathways inside its transformer: The understanding pathway interprets the prompt and other conditioning inputs. These inputs remain fixed during generation. The generation pathway processes the evolving video, sound, or action representation at every denoising step while using the understanding result as context. The transformer contains both understanding and generation computation. With fixed conditioning and precision, the adapter prepares the understanding context once and reuses it during generation. If native FP8 precision changes during denoising, that context is refreshed to match. Video 1 shows how generation traverses the transformer blocks at each denoising step. A 35-step request runs denoising steps 1 through 35. Each step traverses 36 transformer blocks, indexed 0 through 35. After block 35, the scheduler updates the generation state and the next step starts at block 0. After the final denoising step, the pipeline decodes the output. Video 1. Learn how Cosmos 3 Nano streams weights from CPU to GPU Classifier-free guidance (CFG) in Hugging Face combines predictions with and without prompt conditioning at each denoising step. The adapter reuses each streamed block across these predictions instead of transferring its weights for each branch. Transfer can add a control branch, which the automatic low-memory mode handles through the same API. Keep the official Diffusers pipeline The adapter uses the official Diffusers modular pipeline for: Prompt processing Conditioning and latent preparation Sequence preparation The denoising loop and UniPC scheduler Masking and classifier-free guidance output handling VAE decode Safety checking Output conversion Manage memory across the complete request Block offloading alone is not enough for the complete Cosmos pipeline. The adapter applies the following behavior automatically. Reuse fixed understanding work With fixed precision, the understanding pathway runs once for fixed conditioning inputs and its context is reused during denoising. Stream generation blocks Transformer weights remain in system RAM until their block is needed. The active block moves to the GPU, performs its CUDA work for the current denoising step, and makes room for the next block. Guidance predictions share the same block placement whenever possible. Overlap transfers with computation When the GPU has enough headroom, the next block can begin moving while the current block computes. Larger workloads automatically use the safer lower-memory schedule. There is no user-facing transfer schedule to configure. Manage decoding and safety checks VAE processing and safety checking have different memory requirements from denoising. The adapter manages those phases separately and automatically uses memory-efficient VAE execution on constrained cards. Users do not choose device-specific tuning values. Handle larger Transfer requests Transfer Modality performs more guidance work than text-to-video (T2V) and image-to-video (I2V). At 720p on a 12 GB GPU, the adapter automatically selects a lower-memory execution mode. The full GeForce RTX 5070 modality results include its generation time and guardrail settings. Step 3: Generate other modalities ( sound, action, etc ) Reuse pipe, device, and common_video_args from Step 1 for the examples in this section. Replace the input image and video paths with your own files. The prompts are illustrative; use the benchmark scripts for the exact measured inputs. Video-only calls return a list of frames. Calls requesting sound or action return a mapping of the requested outputs. Image-to-video Condition generation on an image with image= . from diffusers.utils import load_image image = load_image("/path/to/conditioning_image.jpg") i2v = pipe( prompt='{"scene":"A vehicle approaches a rockfall on a coastal road"}', image=image, generator=torch.Generator(device=device).manual_seed(1111), output="videos", **common_video_args, ) Video-to-video Pass a source video and choose the conditioning frames for video-to-video (V2V) generation. from diffusers.utils import load_video source_video = load_video("/path/to/source_video.mp4") v2v = pipe( prompt='{"scene":"A robot pours liquid into a cup"}', video=source_video, condition_frame_indexes_vision=[0, 1], condition_video_keep="first", generator=torch.Generator(device=device).manual_seed(0), output="videos", **common_video_args, ) Text-to-video with sound Set enable_sound=True and include an audio description to generate video and sound together. t2v_sound = pipe( prompt=( '{"scene":"A robot arm working in a kitchen",' '"audio_description":"Soft servo whirring and a ceramic clink."}' ), enable_sound=True, generator=torch.Generator(device=device).manual_seed(0), output=["videos", "sound", "sampling_rate"], **common_video_args, ) Image-to-video with sound Combine the image input with enable_sound=True to generate both outputs. i2v_sound = pipe( prompt=( '{"scene":"A vehicle travels along a coastal road",' '"audio_description":"Road noise, wind, and distant waves."}' ), image=image, enable_sound=True, generator=torch.Generator(device=device).manual_seed(0), output=["videos", "sound", "sampling_rate"], **common_video_args, ) Action generation Use CosmosActionCondition to select the action domain and provide the conditioning video. from diffusers import CosmosActionCondition action_result = pipe( prompt="Put the pot to the left of the purple item.", action=CosmosActionCondition( mode="policy", chunk_size=16, domain_name="bridge_orig_lerobot", resolution_tier=480, video=load_video("/path/to/bridge_input.mp4"), view_point="ego_view", ), fps=5, num_inference_steps=30, guidance_scale=1.0, use_system_prompt=False, generator=torch.Generator(device=device).manual_seed(0), output=["videos", "action"], ) Control-guided generation Pass a control video with the control_videos argument. Safety checking remains enabled in this example; the benchmark’s guardrails-off exception is documented with the results. transfer = pipe( prompt='{"scene":"Transform the input using edge guidance"}', negative_prompt="", control_videos={ "edge": load_video("/path/to/control_edge.mp4"), }, num_frames=121, height=720, width=1280, fps=30.0, num_inference_steps=35, guidance_scale=3.0, control_guidance=1.5, generator=torch.Generator(device=device).manual_seed(0), output="videos", ) Diffusers routes each call to the appropriate workflow and loads the required components through the same pipeline. Step 4: Use the FP8 checkpoint Use nvidia/Cosmos3-Nano with the FP8 branch for the dedicated FP8 checkpoint. From the same package directory, install the FP8 extra, which includes NVIDIA Model Optimizer , before loading the checkpoint: uv pip install '.[benchmarks,fp8]' Select the FP8 branch through the same Hub API by passing revision="fp8" : pipe = build_pipeline( "nvidia/Cosmos3-Nano", revision="fp8", config=StreamingConfig(device="cuda:0"), dtype=torch.bfloat16, checkpoint_precision="fp8", ) The adapter uses the checkpoint’s native Diffusers precision policy. W8A8 uses 8-bit weights and 8-bit activations. W8A16 reuses the stored 8-bit weights, dequantizes them for a linear operation, and uses 16-bit activations. The tested Nano video checkpoint selects W8A16 for the first three and last three denoising steps and W8A8 for the middle steps. Note that attention remains BF16 SDPA; the entire pipeline does not run in FP8. Step 5: Choose a GPU and resolution Use Table 1 to choose a starting resolution. The default configuration adapts automatically to the requested resolution, modality, and available GPU memory. GPU class Recommended use 12 GB Start at 240p or 480p for iteration. Full 720p is supported, including Transfer, but can be substantially slower. 16 GB 480p is a practical iteration mode; 720p is supported with automatic memory management. 24 GB Full-resolution generation has more working room and is materially faster in the tested configuration. 32 GB Best measured consumer-GPU latency for the 720p BF16 workload. Table 1. Suggested starting resolutions by GPU memory capacity These are guidance ranges rather than fixed limits. Resolution, frame count, modality, checkpoint precision, available system RAM, and PCIe bandwidth all affect fit and runtime. Step 6: Benchmark setup and results The presented results cover text-to-video across four GeForce RTX cards and all seven generation modalities on the GeForce RTX 5070. Use Table 4 to estimate memory requirements and wait times. Hosts, software revisions, and safety settings can affect latency, so these single-run measurements are not a controlled GPU ranking or a multiseed BF16-versus-FP8 comparison. Reproduce the benchmarks From the package directory used in Step 1, run the BF16 and FP8 benchmarks separately to measure your system. These commands cover all seven modalities and three resolution tiers. Install the FP8 dependency from Step 4 before running the FP8 command. python benchmarks/benchmark_bf16.py --output-dir artifacts/benchmark-bf16 python benchmarks/benchmark_fp8.py --output-dir artifacts/benchmark-fp8 The benchmark guide in benchmarks/README.md explains the pinned inputs, per-case logs, summary tables, --resume , and --preflight-only . Safety checks are enabled by default. Reproducing the labeled Transfer timings requires an explicit Transfer-only run with --transfer-without-guardrails . The FP8 runner records the exact checkpoint revision and uses the native Diffusers policy. Test settings The benchmark workloads use the bundled model-card inputs. Each saved video was checked for its output dimensions, frame count, and frame rate. Sound cases also produced WAV files, and Action cases produced action JSON. Table 2 lists the generation and timing settings. Control BF16 T2V RTX 5070 modalities Output 189 frames, 24 fps 189 frames for video/sound; 17 for Action; 121 at 30 fps for Transfer Resolution tiers 432×240, 848×480, 1280×720 432×240, 848×480, 1280×720; action uses corresponding tiers Denoising 35 UniPC steps, CFG 6, seed 123 35 steps for video/sound/Transfer; 30 for Action; fixed per-modality inputs and seeds Safety Enabled Enabled except the explicitly labeled guardrails-off Transfer rows Timing Pipeline call through returned frames Pipeline call through returned modality tensors Excluded Construction, checkpoint loading, MP4 encoding Construction, checkpoint loading, file encoding Table 2. Generation settings and timing definitions Tested hardware Table 3 lists the tested GPUs. Each host had approximately 128 GB of system RAM. CPU offloading exchanges GPU memory pressure for system RAM use. The measured consumer-GPU hosts had approximately 128 GB of system RAM. Pipeline time includes prompt processing, understanding, denoising, VAE decode, and safety checking, but excludes checkpoint loading and MP4 encoding. Full text-to-video pipeline latency and peak GPU memory across RTX cards Full modality results on RTX 5070 Table 5 lists full generations on the 12 GB RTX 5070 with a 128 GB-class host. FP8 uses the checkpoint’s native W8A16 first/last-three schedule and W8A8 middle steps. Prompt and output safety checks are enabled for both precisions except in the labeled Transfer rows. items.raw_text: Simulation / Modeling / Design How to Run NVIDIA Cosmos 3 on Local AI Devices Using Hugging Face Diffusers Nov 24, 2026 By Atharva Joshi and Jibin Varghese Like Discuss (0) L T F R E AI-Generated Summary NVIDIA Cosmos 3 Nano is a world foundation model that generates videos from text, images, and other inputs to support physical AI development. The Cosmos-Framework offloading package enables running Cosmos 3 Nano on GPUs with as little as 12 GB of VRAM by storing model weights in system RAM and transferring them to the GPU as needed during generation. An FP8 checkpoint with native mixed precision reduces peak GPU memory usage while maintaining BF16 scaled dot-product attention for the attention layers. The adapter supports seven generation modalities including text-to-video, image-to-video, video-to-video, sound generation, action generation, and control-guided generation through the official Diffusers modular pipeline. Benchmark results across GeForce RTX 5070, 5080, 4090, and 5090 show pipeline latency and peak memory usage for each resolution and modality, with the RTX 5070 completing 720p text-to-video in 2,624.9 seconds at 9.94 GiB peak memory using BF16. Next Steps Download the Cosmos 3 Nano checkpoint and its FP8 branch on Hugging Face. Find examples and code in the Cosmos-Framework offloading package . Review the Diffusers memory optimization guide for CPU offloading and the Cosmos 3 pipeline documentation for supported generation workflows. Powered by NVIDIA Nemotron. AI-generated content may summarize information incompletely. Verify important information. Learn more Running video generation models locally can be challenging when model weights and intermediate data exceed available GPU memory. NVIDIA Cosmos 3 Nano is a world foundation model that generates videos from text, images, and other inputs to support physical AI development. Learn more about NVIDIA Cosmos for physical AI . This tutorial walks you through how to run Cosmos 3 Nano on a GPU with as little as 12 GB of VRAM by storing most model weights in system RAM and transferring them to the GPU as needed. Using Hugging Face Diffusers, you’ll generate your first video, explore sound and additional input types, and use an FP8 checkpoint to further reduce memory requirements. This streaming adapter builds on top of the native group offloading approach from the Hugging Face library to enable generation on a smaller GPU. The tradeoff is that this requires increased system RAM use and PCIe transfers for a smaller GPU-memory requirement. Note that this approach does not provide interactive latency or stream weights directly from disk during inference. Step 1: Generate your first video Use an existing Linux environment with Python 3.12 and a CUDA-enabled PyTorch build compatible with your GPU. The tested consumer-GPU hosts had approximately 128 GB of system RAM; this is not a measured minimum. Clone Cosmos-Framework and install its standalone offloading package in your active environment. Run all examples and benchmark commands below from the package directory: git clone https://github.com/NVIDIA/cosmos-framework.git cd cosmos-framework/packages/diffusers-cpu-offloading uv pip install '.[benchmarks]' Pass the Hugging Face repository ID directly to build_pipeline . The first load downloads the checkpoint. Subsequent loads reuse cached files. Safety checking is enabled by default. import torch from cosmos3_streaming import StreamingConfig, build_pipeline device = "cuda:0" config = StreamingConfig(device=device) pipe = build_pipeline( "nvidia/Cosmos3-Nano", config=config, dtype=torch.bfloat16, ) With no revision argument, the BF16 load uses the repository’s default branch. The default configuration chooses appropriate memory-saving behavior automatically. Start with BF16 and PyTorch scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) , the baseline used on all four tested GPUs. Set the video options This example generates 189 frames at 720p. For faster iteration on a 12 GB GPU, change height and width to 480 and 848, or 240 and 432. common_video_args = { "negative_prompt": "", "num_frames": 189, "height": 720, "width": 1280, "fps": 24.0, "num_inference_steps": 35, "guidance_scale": 6.0, "add_resolution_template": False, "add_duration_template": False, } Generate and save the video Next, generate and save the video using the following script: t2v = pipe( prompt='{"scene":"A robot arm working in a kitchen"}', generator=torch.Generator(device=device).manual_seed(123), output="videos", **common_video_args, ) # Save the returned video frames as an MP4 file: from diffusers.utils import export_to_video export_to_video(t2v, "cosmos3_t2v.mp4", fps=common_video_args["fps"]) Step 2: Offload weights storage The central idea is to store model weights in system RAM and use the GPU for computation. To run large models within tight VRAM limits, this execution model manages memory and compute across the CPU and GPU in four ways: Checkpoint weights that are not currently needed remain in system RAM, in BF16 or the checkpoint’s FP8 representation. The next transformer block is transferred to the GPU when required. Every matrix multiplication and attention operation runs on CUDA. The adapter manages memory for denoising, the variational autoencoder (VAE) that encodes and decodes video, and safety checking. With this approach, system RAM acts as the backing store for model weights. More demanding requests, including 720p Transfer on a 12 GB GPU, use an automatic lower-memory execution mode while keeping model computation on CUDA. Move weights from system RAM to the GPU Next, move weights from system RAM to the GPU. Figure 1 shows the path from checkpoint storage to GPU computation. Checkpoint files remain on disk between runs. During generation, system RAM is the backing store for weights that are not currently on the GPU. This is why a fast SSD helps with model loading, while sufficient system RAM and PCIe bandwidth matter during generation. Figure 1. Streaming model weights from system RAM to the GPU enables NVIDIA Cosmos 3 Nano generation without keeping the full model in GPU memory Reuse understanding context during generation Diffusers provides sequential, model-level, and group-level CPU offloading to move model components between CPU and GPU memory. The Cosmos adapter builds on those mechanisms and coordinates when the model’s understanding and generation pathways run. NVIDIA Cosmos 3 , an open omnimodal world foundation model for physical AI, has two complementary pathways inside its transformer: The understanding pathway interprets the prompt and other conditioning inputs. These inputs remain fixed during generation. The generation pathway processes the evolving video, sound, or action representation at every denoising step while using the understanding result as context. The transformer contains both understanding and generation computation. With fixed conditioning and precision, the adapter prepares the understanding context once and reuses it during generation. If native FP8 precision changes during denoising, that context is refreshed to match. Video 1 shows how generation traverses the transformer blocks at each denoising step. A 35-step request runs denoising steps 1 through 35. Each step traverses 36 transformer blocks, indexed 0 through 35. After block 35, the scheduler updates the generation state and the next step starts at block 0. After the final denoising step, the pipeline decodes the output. Video 1. Learn how Cosmos 3 Nano streams weights from CPU to GPU Classifier-free guidance (CFG) in Hugging Face combines predictions with and without prompt conditioning at each denoising step. The adapter reuses each streamed block across these predictions instead of transferring its weights for each branch. Transfer can add a control branch, which the automatic low-memory mode handles through the same API. Keep the official Diffusers pipeline The adapter uses the official Diffusers modular pipeline for: Prompt processing Conditioning and latent preparation Sequence preparation The denoising loop and UniPC scheduler Masking and classifier-free guidance output handling VAE decode Safety checking Output conversion Manage memory across the complete request Block offloading alone is not enough for the complete Cosmos pipeline. The adapter applies the following behavior automatically. Reuse fixed understanding work With fixed precision, the understanding pathway runs once for fixed conditioning inputs and its context is reused during denoising. Stream generation blocks Transformer weights remain in system RAM until their block is needed. The active block moves to the GPU, performs its CUDA work for the current denoising step, and makes room for the next block. Guidance predictions share the same block placement whenever possible. Overlap transfers with computation When the GPU has enough headroom, the next block can begin moving while the current block computes. Larger workloads automatically use the safer lower-memory schedule. There is no user-facing transfer schedule to configure. Manage decoding and safety checks VAE processing and safety checking have different memory requirements from denoising. The adapter manages those phases separately and automatically uses memory-efficient VAE execution on constrained cards. Users do not choose device-specific tuning values. Handle larger Transfer requests Transfer Modality performs more guidance work than text-to-video (T2V) and image-to-video (I2V). At 720p on a 12 GB GPU, the adapter automatically selects a lower-memory execution mode. The full GeForce RTX 5070 modality results include its generation time and guardrail settings. Step 3: Generate other modalities ( sound, action, etc ) Reuse pipe, device, and common_video_args from Step 1 for the examples in this section. Replace the input image and video paths with your own files. The prompts are illustrative; use the benchmark scripts for the exact measured inputs. Video-only calls return a list of frames. Calls requesting sound or action return a mapping of the requested outputs. Image-to-video Condition generation on an image with image= . from diffusers.utils import load_image image = load_image("/path/to/conditioning_image.jpg") i2v = pipe( prompt='{"scene":"A vehicle approaches a rockfall on a coastal road"}', image=image, generator=torch.Generator(device=device).manual_seed(1111), output="videos", **common_video_args, ) Video-to-video Pass a source video and choose the conditioning frames for video-to-video (V2V) generation. from diffusers.utils import load_video source_video = load_video("/path/to/source_video.mp4") v2v = pipe( prompt='{"scene":"A robot pours liquid into a cup"}', video=source_video, condition_frame_indexes_vision=[0, 1], condition_video_keep="first", generator=torch.Generator(device=device).manual_seed(0), output="videos", **common_video_args, ) Text-to-video with sound Set enable_sound=True and include an audio description to generate video and sound together. t2v_sound = pipe( prompt=( '{"scene":"A robot arm working in a kitchen",' '"audio_description":"Soft servo whirring and a ceramic clink."}' ), enable_sound=True, generator=torch.Generator(device=device).manual_seed(0), output=["videos", "sound", "sampling_rate"], **common_video_args, ) Image-to-video with sound Combine the image input with enable_sound=True to generate both outputs. i2v_sound = pipe( prompt=( '{"scene":"A vehicle travels along a coastal road",' '"audio_description":"Road noise, wind, and distant waves."}' ), image=image, enable_sound=True, generator=torch.Generator(device=device).manual_seed(0), output=["videos", "sound", "sampling_rate"], **common_video_args, ) Action generation Use CosmosActionCondition to select the action domain and provide the conditioning video. from diffusers import CosmosActionCondition action_result = pipe( prompt="Put the pot to the left of the purple item.", action=CosmosActionCondition( mode="policy", chunk_size=16, domain_name="bridge_orig_lerobot", resolution_tier=480, video=load_video("/path/to/bridge_input.mp4"), view_point="ego_view", ), fps=5, num_inference_steps=30, guidance_scale=1.0, use_system_prompt=False, generator=torch.Generator(device=device).manual_seed(0), output=["videos", "action"], ) Control-guided generation Pass a control video with the control_videos argument. Safety checking remains enabled in this example; the benchmark’s guardrails-off exception is documented with the results. transfer = pipe( prompt='{"scene":"Transform the input using edge guidance"}', negative_prompt="", control_videos={ "edge": load_video("/path/to/control_edge.mp4"), }, num_frames=121, height=720, width=1280, fps=30.0, num_inference_steps=35, guidance_scale=3.0, control_guidance=1.5, generator=torch.Generator(device=device).manual_seed(0), output="videos", ) Diffusers routes each call to the appropriate workflow and loads the required components through the same pipeline. Step 4: Use the FP8 checkpoint Use nvidia/Cosmos3-Nano with the FP8 branch for the dedicated FP8 checkpoint. From the same package directory, install the FP8 extra, which includes NVIDIA Model Optimizer , before loading the checkpoint: uv pip install '.[benchmarks,fp8]' Select the FP8 branch through the same Hub API by passing revision="fp8" : pipe = build_pipeline( "nvidia/Cosmos3-Nano", revision="fp8", config=StreamingConfig(device="cuda:0"), dtype=torch.bfloat16, checkpoint_precision="fp8", ) The adapter uses the checkpoint’s native Diffusers precision policy. W8A8 uses 8-bit weights and 8-bit activations. W8A16 reuses the stored 8-bit weights, dequantizes them for a linear operation, and uses 16-bit activations. The tested Nano video checkpoint selects W8A16 for the first three and last three denoising steps and W8A8 for the middle steps. Note that attention remains BF16 SDPA; the entire pipeline does not run in FP8. Step 5: Choose a GPU and resolution Use Table 1 to choose a starting resolution. The default configuration adapts automatically to the requested resolution, modality, and available GPU memory. GPU class Recommended use 12 GB Start at 240p or 480p for iteration. Full 720p is supported, including Transfer, but can be substantially slower. 16 GB 480p is a practical iteration mode; 720p is supported with automatic memory management. 24 GB Full-resolution generation has more working room and is materially faster in the tested configuration. 32 GB Best measured consumer-GPU latency for the 720p BF16 workload. Table 1. Suggested starting resolutions by GPU memory capacity These are guidance ranges rather than fixed limits. Resolution, frame count, modality, checkpoint precision, available system RAM, and PCIe bandwidth all affect fit and runtime. Step 6: Benchmark setup and results The presented results cover text-to-video across four GeForce RTX cards and all seven generation modalities on the GeForce RTX 5070. Use Table 4 to estimate memory requirements and wait times. Hosts, software revisions, and safety settings can affect latency, so these single-run measurements are not a controlled GPU ranking or a multiseed BF16-versus-FP8 comparison. Reproduce the benchmarks From the package directory used in Step 1, run the BF16 and FP8 benchmarks separately to measure your system. These commands cover all seven modalities and three resolution tiers. Install the FP8 dependency from Step 4 before running the FP8 command. python benchmarks/benchmark_bf16.py --output-dir artifacts/benchmark-bf16 python benchmarks/benchmark_fp8.py --output-dir artifacts/benchmark-fp8 The benchmark guide in benchmarks/README.md explains the pinned inputs, per-case logs, summary tables, --resume , and --preflight-only . Safety checks are enabled by default. Reproducing the labeled Transfer timings requires an explicit Transfer-only run with --transfer-without-guardrails . The FP8 runner records the exact checkpoint revision and uses the native Diffusers policy. Test settings The benchmark workloads use the bundled model-card inputs. Each saved video was checked for its output dimensions, frame count, and frame rate. Sound cases also produced WAV files, and Action cases produced action JSON. items.content: Back to Articles Hugging Face and OpenRouter join forces to make open-weight models easy to run Published November 16, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 119 +113 Célina Hanouti celinah Follow Victor Mustar victor Follow Bertrand Chevrier kramp Follow Lucain Pouget Wauplin Follow Pierric Cistac pierric Follow Eliott Coyac coyotte508 Follow Julien Chaumond julien-c Follow Hugging Face and OpenRouter are teaming up to make open-weight models easy to run. Every major open-weight release is already being published on the Hugging Face Hub, and OpenRouter serves those models at scale, routing each request across 80+ providers based on live measurements of each one. Together, every open-weight model on the Hub that a provider serves can be called with your Hugging Face token, through the same API, with the best provider picked for each request. Today, we are switching Inference Providers from our own custom router to OpenRouter's. Requests made to language models now go through OpenRouter, which picks the best provider for each call based on live price, speed and reliability, and retries on another provider if the first one fails. Your code stays the same. Run them with the tools you already use The router supports OpenAI's Chat Completions and Responses APIs and Anthropic's Messages API for every chat model, whatever the provider behind it. Pick your coding agent or SDK and a model, then copy the steps, or copy the whole setup as a prompt for your agent: Setup guides for Claude Code , Codex , OpenCode , Pi and Hermes Agent The same Hugging Face token also gives you storage with Storage Buckets , compute with Jobs and dedicated inference with Inference Endpoints . PRO, Team and Enterprise plans include monthly credits for compute and inference. How open-weight models are used On OpenRouter, open-weight models went from 26.8% of the tokens served in October 2025 to 71.7% at the end of September 2026, after peaking at 77.5% in July ( OpenRouter, October 2026 ). Over the same period, weekly open-weight volume grew more than 60-fold, against almost tenfold for closed models. This week, the most used model on OpenRouter is an open-weight one, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, with 59.2 trillion tokens ( rankings ). Open-weight models cost about four times less on average: $0.28 per million input tokens and $1.62 per million output tokens, against $1.27 and $6.36 for closed models. The best open-weight models still trail the best proprietary ones on the hardest benchmarks. On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index , Kimi K3.1 Pro, the best open-weight model, scores 46 against 65 for Claude Fable 5.2, at about a seventh of the cost per task ($3.68 against $26.54). For a lot of workloads, that trade-off is worth it. Its routing is based on live measurements of every provider across that traffic. OpenRouter recently rebuilt its provider routing : instead of only looking at the lowest list price, it sends each request to the provider with the best mix of price, speed and reliability. When a provider slows down or starts failing, traffic moves away from it until it recovers, and a failed try is retried on the next best provider inside the same call. In OpenRouter's measurements, the new routing cut capacity errors by 46% and improved time to first token by 16.9% and throughput by 16.3%. Before, Inference Providers picked one provider for your request and returned its error if it failed. Now, the request is retried on another provider. Breaking change: custom provider keys Requests to language models now go through OpenRouter and are billed to your Hugging Face account or organization, so you can no longer use your own API key for a provider with these models. You can still pick a provider with a suffix on the model id ( model:provider ) or turn providers off in your settings, and your code stays the same. items.content: Back to Articles DaisyRose-27B: Pushing the Frontier of Post-Training Efficiency Team Article Published November 18, 2026 Upvote 29 +23 Jason Chen jzsc Follow RadixArk Today we are releasing DaisyRose-27B , RadixArk’s first model, built on Qwen3.8-27B and trained with reinforcement learning using Miles . We trained it on long-horizon agent tasks with sessions up to 1M tokens, with just 1,200 curated tasks in 18 days on 144 H200 GPUs. DaisyRose-27B improves Terminal-Bench 4.1 pass@1 from 5.6% to 12.0% . Beyond Terminal-Bench 4.1, it also delivers gains on a variety of other reasoning, instruction following, and coding benchmarks. The checkpoints are available under Apache 2.0 : BF16 FP8 NVFP4 The model retains Qwen3.8-27B’s architecture, tokenizer, chat template, image understanding, and 256K-token context window . The longer training sessions use harness summarization to span multiple trajectories. See the model card for model properties and inference settings. Run DaisyRose-27B We recommend serving DaisyRose-27B with SGLang and DSpark speculative decoding. The SGLang cookbook provides launch configurations for different GPUs and checkpoint formats. After starting the server with the served model name DaisyRose-27B on port 30000 , you can send a request using the OpenAI Python client: from openai import OpenAI client = OpenAI( base_url= "http://localhost:30000/v1" , api_key= "none" , ) response = client.chat.completions.create( model= "DaisyRose-27B" , messages=[ { "role" : "user" , "content" : "How many positive divisors does 360 have?" , } ], temperature= 1.0 , top_p= 0.95 , extra_body={ "top_k" : 20 , "min_p" : 0.0 }, ) print (response.choices[ 0 ].message.reasoning_content) print (response.choices[ 0 ].message.content) The model thinks before answering by default. Its reasoning is returned in reasoning_content , and its final answer in content . These settings follow the model card’s quickstart . Benchmark results Benchmark Qwen3.8-27B DaisyRose-27B Terminal Bench 4.1 5.6 12.0 Terminal Bench 2.1 73.0 75.5 DeepSWE v1.1 42.2 46.2 SWE Bench Pro v2 91.3 94.7 HLE (text-only) 33.9 34.3 IFBench 79.5 82.4 GPQA Diamond 89.2 90.7 DaisyRose-27B scores higher than the original Qwen3.8-27B model on every benchmark above. The largest gain is on Terminal Bench 4.1, where pass@1 rises from 5.6% to 12.0%. Scores use the higher of the BF16 and FP8 runs for each benchmark; the two differ by less than one point wherever both were evaluated. The model card includes comparison sources and evaluation settings. Three parts of the training setup made this release possible: carefully designed tasks, an efficient training backend, and reliable sandboxes. High-quality training data We built the tasks in partnership with Eigent AI , starting from its large pool of tasks in machine learning, software engineering, science, and other fields. Together we built thousands of candidates. About 1,200 made it into the final training set. We selected tasks using three criteria: Each task targets a mistake the original model makes. We ran Qwen3.8-27B on every task and redesigned each one around the mistakes we wanted the model to stop making. We then adjusted the difficulty until the solve rate fell within a useful learning range. Each task requires several interdependent steps. The agent has to reason, plan, and execute across a long job. Each attempt gets up to 1.5 hours in a sandbox, with more than 100 tool calls and more than 256K output tokens. Tasks must reward actually solving the problem. We reviewed every task alongside the model’s attempts. Tasks that could be passed without solving the intended problem, or that contained a design flaw, were fixed or removed. Efficient training backend RadixArk trained DaisyRose-27B with Miles, our open-source reinforcement learning framework for large-scale model post-training, in fully asynchronous mode: the agent keeps working while the model learns, and neither waits for the other. While 128 H200s run the inference on agent tasks, 16 more run the trainer and learn from the trajectories. After every step, the updated model goes out to the 128 GPUs that run the agent. The learning runs on our internal training backend, which is built for agent training: each step learns from a handful of very long sessions, some as long as 1M tokens, folded into multiple trajectories via harness summarization. 57% lower training cost. On this release, 37% of each GPU’s peak compute went into useful training work (model FLOPs utilization, or MFU) on our backend. The open-source trainer, built on Megatron, reached 16% on comparable runs. So the same training needs 57% less GPU time. The gain is even larger on mixture-of-experts models: 6.2× on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, and more than 10× on the roughly 300B-parameter GLM-5.3-Flash. 2× faster end to end. Counting the time the agent spends on its tasks, the release run trained on about 16,800 tokens per second across its 144 GPUs. The open-source trainer reached about 8,300 on the same GPUs. Stable over weeks. The release run trained for weeks on 144 H200s, 63,000 GPU-hours in total. From the first step to the last, its speed and efficiency held steady. Every training step of the DaisyRose-27B release run on 144 H200s, plotted against total training time. Dashed lines: the open-source trainer on comparable runs. Robust sandbox service Every training attempt runs in a sandbox: a fresh copy of the task’s environment where the agent runs commands, edits files, and is then graded. Our service is built on the open-source AgentENV project, to which we also contribute fixes. Between mid-September and mid-November, it ran about 944,000 sandboxes for this project, with up to 1,566 running concurrently . The service grew from one machine to as many as 12. We shipped ten upgrades to it, nearly all while training was running. Across all nine weeks, 99% of sandbox creations succeeded; since late October, that figure has exceeded 99.95%. Cloud infrastructure costs for the project’s sandboxes were about 80% lower than running the same sandboxes with popular cloud sandbox providers. One way we keep costs down is to let each sandbox’s memory allocation grow and shrink with its actual usage, allowing more sandboxes to share each machine. Try the model or train your own Download DaisyRose-27B , follow the SGLang serving guide , or use Miles to train your own agents. We’d like to hear how DaisyRose-27B performs on your tasks, including where it falls short. Share your setup and results in the model’s Community tab. We thank Eigent AI for working closely with us on training data, and the Qwen team for creating Qwen3.8-27B. We also thank the Miles and SGLang communities, along with other open-source projects including slime, AgentENV, and Harbor. Adapted from the original RadixArk article . items.content: Back to Articles 180B Parameters, 32GB of RAM: Pushing MoE Inference to the Limit with Transformers Published November 18, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 40 +34 Tarek Ziadé tarekziade Follow Streaming MoE experts directly from SSD gets within 6% of Strata on token generation. I've been trying to rely less on online models and run bigger ones locally. At home I have a PC with two RTX 4090s (let's call it Orthrus - the two-headed hound of Greek mythology), and for work I have a MacBook M5 with 32G of unified memory. Orthrus runs on Windows 11, because my kids play games all the time. I had a dual boot with Ubuntu, but their games ended up taking most of the two terabytes of disk. I am also a huge fan of RMD (rooms moving development): one hour in the kitchen sipping my coffee, two hours at my office desk, then the sofa. A fixed desktop tower is not for me. My first experiment was to run Qwen 3.8 27B with llama.app on Orthrus and use it from my laptop through pi . That model does the coding tasks, an online model like Opus does the orchestration, and the second RTX runs a FIM model for auto-completion in Neovim. When I talked about this on social networks, I got very strong feedback: use Strata with Qwen3.8-Flash-Next . What is Strata? Strata is an inference engine for MoE models like Qwen. Only the hot experts stay in VRAM, the rest goes to RAM, or even to disk. Experts are 90%+ of a MoE model's weights, so a 180B model like this one can run on a GPU with much less memory. Like my RTX 4090! It works on a laptop too, and I stumbled on this blog post doing exactly that: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on a 32 GB Mac M4, faster than llama.cpp , at 13.5 tok/s. That's too slow for how I use coding agents, but it's an interesting itch to scratch. A whole range of MoE models don't fit in a MacBook's unified memory and could run at a decent speed. How do other engines offload? Before committing to Strata, I looked at what llama.cpp, vLLM and Transformers do when a MoE model doesn't fit. Three questions matter: where do the experts live, where does the expert matmul run, and what moves on each token? llama.cpp maps the GGUF file with mmap and can keep the experts on the CPU ( --cpu-moe , --n-cpu-moe N , -ot "exps=CPU" , or --fit on to pick for you). Those experts are also computed on the CPU, so only the activations cross PCIe, never the weights. Great when the experts fit in RAM. When they don't, the page cache thrashes. A GPU expert cache ( --moe-cache-mib ) just landed, but it fragments the graph (2 splits per token become 50) and loses ~10% even when everything fits. vLLM 's --cpu-offload-gb N puts N GB of weights in pinned RAM, and kernels read them in place over PCIe. For a MoE layer, that's only the routed experts, but nothing is cached: a hot expert crosses PCIe again on every token, and there's no disk tier. By default the offloaded weights include dense layers, read on every token; --cpu-offload-params experts keeps it to the experts. That fits vLLM's big batches, which touch almost every expert anyway, less so one user on one GPU. Transformers offloads through Accelerate ( device_map="auto" , offload_folder ), one module at a time: hooks copy its weights to the GPU before forward . For a MoE, that module is a layer's whole expert bank, so every token copies every expert of every offloaded layer to use 8 or 10 of them. No cache, no notion of routing. And on a Mac, CPU and GPU share the same memory, so "offload to CPU" frees nothing. I ran all of them on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on one A10G (24 GB), with plenty of RAM, and Harry Mellor reran vLLM with better flags: Engine Decode (tok/s) Strata, Q8_0 82 - 88 llama.cpp, Q8_0, --fit on 63 - 64 llama.cpp, BF16, --fit on 35 - 36 vLLM, FP8, --cpu-offload-gb 16 --cpu-offload-params experts 20.1 vLLM, FP8, same flags, --enforce-eager 14.7 vLLM, FP8, --cpu-offload-gb 16 9.7 vLLM, BF16, --cpu-offload-gb 50 --cpu-offload-params experts 7.3 vLLM, BF16, --cpu-offload-gb 50 3.3 Transformers + Accelerate 0.16 Offloading only the experts doubles vLLM's speed, and FP8 helps on top (half the bytes per expert, more of the model on the GPU). vLLM's other offload backend, which copies groups of layers ahead of time, ran under 1 tok/s. If the experts fit in RAM, llama.cpp is hard to beat. If they don't, you have to stream only what the router picks, through a bounded cache, fast enough that the SSD is the bottleneck and not Python, ideally reusing the model's fast expert kernels. That's Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on a 32 GB Mac, and Transformers couldn't do it out of the box. Making Qwen3.8-Flash-Next work on my 32 GB Mac with Transformers Strata was already too slow for me on the laptop, and Transformers was not going to beat it anytime soon. But the Accelerate path was so far off that I wanted to try fixing offloading in Transformers itself, with the big model on my laptop as the target, knowing it would probably stay too slow for how I work. All of the code was built with AI: the Transformers PR, the model-specific package and the Metal kernels. My part was choosing what to try, reading the profiles, and deciding what to keep. Everything is in a Space: tarekziade/moe-expert-streaming . Start small I started with OLMoE-1B-7B , which fits in memory, so I could compare every token with vanilla Transformers. First version: experts on disk, an LRU cache on the device, and a Python loop running one expert at a time. With every expert already cached, it did 10.1 tok/s. Vanilla did ~32. The I/O was fine, my loop was not: vanilla uses grouped_mm , which runs all the experts of a layer in one kernel. The fix, and the key idea of this project, was to turn the cache into a slot pool : one preallocated device tensor shared by all layers, plus a per-layer table from expert id to slot. Remap the router's expert ids to slots and the pool looks like a regular expert bank, so grouped_mm runs on it as is. No custom expert matmul needed. That got it to 34.6 tok/s, against 38.1 for vanilla. experts_offload I then turned the standalone loader into an option of from_pretrained , in huggingface/transformers#50717 . Experts mapped to "disk" go through the streaming path instead of Accelerate's offload: the loader skips their tensors and MoE layers switch to an offloaded implementation. Misses are read by 8 I/O threads, one contiguous read per expert. The next two layers' routers run early on the current hidden states to guess which experts to prefetch. Experts can be quantized offline so reads are smaller. It works for MoE models with the standard experts layout. The API is still being discussed with the Transformers maintainers. The device_map form came out of that, and quantized experts will probably go through the per-layer quantization plan of #50245 rather than their own option. Running 121 GB of experts on a 32 GB Mac Qwen3.8-Flash-Next has 48 layers of 512 experts (10 active), 121 GB in FP8. Streaming them isn't enough: there's also a 51 GB n-gram embedding table that needs its own disk path. So: experts quantized to 3 bits: 49 GB on disk, 12 GiB cached on the device dense layers in 8 bits (~5.4 GB, +0.2% perplexity vs BF16) the n-gram table stays on disk, rows read when needed The conversion takes ~5 hours. After loading, it uses ~18 GiB, and a 6K prompt peaks at 25.4 GiB. That's about the limit: I have to close the browser, or macOS starts swapping. The model-specific bits (the n-gram table, Metal kernels) live in a small package, moe-expert-streaming , on top of the PR. The first version ran at about 10 tok/s. Then I installed Strata on the same M5, with the same prompts: Transformers Strata Gap Decode, 200 tokens 10.0 tok/s 14.8 1.5x Prefill, 4K prompt 68 tok/s 220 3.2x Decode after a 6K document 7.3 tok/s 13.7 1.9x Strata 0.1.60 used IQ3_XXS experts. Both ran greedy, with thinking, MTP and speculative drafts off, and 1,024-token prefill chunks. The full setup and raw results are on the Space's details page . I also tried vllm-metal , vLLM on Apple GPUs through MLX, which recently got expert offloading. It streams the routed experts from an MLX checkpoint through a bounded cache, like this project. But it can't run Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on 32 GB, for the n-gram reason above: only the experts are streamed, and the n-gram tables stay in memory. That's 32 GB in the MLX checkpoints on the Hub, before the ~5 GB of dense layers and any expert cache. Closing the gap Most of the time wasn't spent on experts. Here's what helped: Committing GPU work early. PyTorch on MPS holds small kernels until the next sync, so the GPU idled while Python worked. Forcing a commit after each block gave +10%. This should really be fixed in PyTorch. Metal kernels for the parts without a fast path on macOS: Gated DeltaNet and the hyper-connections. Strata's own weights. I switched to Strata's GGUF weights , reducing dense weight traffic from 5.4 GB to 3.9 GB per token and individual expert size from 2.15 MB to 1.75 MB, with a separate cache pool for each expert size. Prefill , we went from 68 to ~228 tok/s using bigger chunks, and reading the next layer's experts while the current layer is being computed. Long documents : attention over the indexer's selected blocks only, and a KV cache that grows in place instead of being copied at every token. Misses : Strata doesn't hide them, it waits like I do, and no cache policy beat LRU by much. What helped was reading just one guessed expert per layer, while the SSD would otherwise be idle. Here's one MoE layer for one token, as it runs now: These are the final results after these optimizations on the same M5 with the same prompts: Transformers Strata Gap Decode, 200 tokens 13.9 tok/s 14.8 1.06x Prefill, 4K prompt 228 tok/s 220 1.0x Decode after a 6K document 12.4 tok/s 13.7 1.1x That's about 6% behind Strata on short decode, with slightly faster prefill, all through Transformers. Most of what's left is host round trips, ~10 ms per token. Waking up after a sync is only ~1 ms of that. The rest is the GPU running dry while Python queues the next layer. Strata queues the whole token's work up front, and the GPU waits on a Metal shared event at each layer while the host reads experts. PyTorch doesn't expose that. I tried to fake it with a kernel spinning on a flag the CPU writes, and the GPU took anywhere from a second to never to see the write. The real fix would be a native op on PyTorch's MPS stream, with a risk of hangs, so I haven't built it. Conclusion It runs at ~14 tok/s, close to Strata, and it's still too slow for how I use coding agents. Orthrus keeps doing the real work. Transformers didn't beat Strata, and closing the last ~6% would take deeper changes in the stack, starting with control over that per-layer sync, which PyTorch doesn't give you today. The interesting part is how it got that close: streaming only the routed experts, a bounded cache that grouped_mm runs on as is, and a few targeted Metal kernels. There's no C++ extension in the project: just Python, Metal kernels compiled at runtime with torch.mps.compile_shader , and prebuilt kernels from the Hub . All the Metal kernels written for this experiment are now published on the Hub , and the project loads them from there. Beating Strata was never the only goal, though. Building this was a great way to learn how MoEs and LLMs work from a systems perspective: how sparse the routing really is, how much an expert cache buys you, where memory bandwidth goes per token, and how much time the host and the GPU spend waiting on each other. Transformers makes all of that easy to poke at, one module at a time. The generic expert streaming implementation is in huggingface/transformers#50717 , and the benchmarks are in the Space . Feedback on the approach and the API is welcome. Thanks to Pedro, Lysandre and Arthur for their excellent feedback, and to Harry for helping test vLLM. Finally, thanks to Niko Veit for Strata . Strata set the bar for what's possible with expert streaming on consumer hardware, and having those numbers to chase is what pushed this work as far as it went. items.title: Rumble-2-Flash: an open 0.5B speech model for 40+ languages
items.summary: Back to Articles Rumble-2-Flash: an open 0.5B speech model for 40+ languages Published November 18, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 25 +19 Reson8 reson8-thomas Follow Reson8 Mark 't Hart MarktHart Follow Reson8 Eustache Le Bihan eustlb Follow Eric Bezzam bezzam Follow Today we're open sourcing Rumble-2-Flash under the Apache 2.0 license. It's a 0.5B-parameter speech recognition model for 40+ languages that competes with models 3-60x its size. Runs anywhere : native support in 🤗 Transformers and vLLM, no custom code 40+ languages : automatic language detection Output control : numbers as digits or words, fillers, verbatim repeats, forced language Extremely fast : an hour of audio in about half a second, with over 7,000 RTFx on full batches Holds up on real phone calls : on par with NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe (30B) on a 302-hour call-centre benchmark Quickstart Transcribe with 🤗 Transformers uv pip install torch transformers accelerate from transformers import AutoProcessor, AutoModel
items.content: Back to Articles Rumble-2-Flash: an open 0.5B speech model for 40+ languages Published November 18, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 25 +19 Reson8 reson8-thomas Follow Reson8 Mark 't Hart MarktHart Follow Reson8 Eustache Le Bihan eustlb Follow Eric Bezzam bezzam Follow Today we're open sourcing Rumble-2-Flash under the Apache 2.0 license. It's a 0.5B-parameter speech recognition model for 40+ languages that competes with models 3-60x its size. Runs anywhere : native support in 🤗 Transformers and vLLM, no custom code 40+ languages : automatic language detection Output control : numbers as digits or words, fillers, verbatim repeats, forced language Extremely fast : an hour of audio in about half a second, with over 7,000 RTFx on full batches Holds up on real phone calls : on par with NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe (30B) on a 302-hour call-centre benchmark Quickstart Transcribe with 🤗 Transformers uv pip install torch transformers accelerate from transformers import AutoProcessor, AutoModelForMultimodalLM model_id = "Reson8/Rumble-2-Flash" processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id) model = AutoModelForMultimodalLM.from_pretrained(model_id, device_map= "auto" ) inputs = processor.apply_transcription_request( audio= "https://hf.co/datasets/hf-internal-testing/dummy-audio-samples/resolve/main/bcn_weather.mp3" , language= "English" , # omit to detect automatically ).to(model.device, dtype=model.dtype) output = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens= 512 ) generated = output[:, inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[- 1 ]:] print (processor.decode(generated, return_format= "transcription_only" )[ 0 ]) # return_format="parsed" if detecting language audio accepts a local path, a URL, a NumPy array, or a list of these. How it's built Rumble-2-Flash uses the Qwen3-ASR architecture for day-0 support. If your stack runs Transformers or vLLM, it runs Rumble-2-Flash, with no forked runtime or trust_remote_code . To find out how small a model could get before accuracy dropped off, we distilled Rumble-2, our larger production model, into it with on-policy distillation. The student doesn't train on transcripts the teacher wrote. It transcribes the audio itself, and the teacher grades that transcript token by token: at every position, it gives its own probability for what should come next, and the student learns to match it. Because the student learns from its own outputs, it gets corrected on exactly the mistakes it makes, with feedback on every token instead of one score per clip. On-policy distillation normally requires teacher and student to share a tokenizer, and ours don't: choosing Qwen3-ASR meant taking its vocabulary too. GOLD removes that restriction. It merges tokens where the two tokenizers split the text differently, so both models are compared over the same text. Tokens that exist in both vocabularies are compared directly, and the rest by their sorted probabilities. On-policy distillation with GOLD Results Accuracy for its size On the Open ASR Leaderboard multilingual track, Rumble-2-Flash averages a 6.96% error rate across Chinese, German, French, Italian, Spanish, Portuguese, Hindi, Dutch and English. That's better than Meta's omniASR-LLM 7B, a model 15x larger, and ahead of Whisper large-v3. On the English track it averages 6.6% WER . The best score for its size Speed Rumble-2-Flash is also fast. Its throughput depends on how full the batches are: on the larger datasets in HF's Open ASR Leaderboard, where batches stay full, it reaches over 7,000 RTFx . That's an hour of audio in about half a second. Real phone calls Clean audio is easy. Phone calls are compressed and noisy, and often have speakers with very different accents. On AppTek's call-centre benchmark (302 hours of helpline calls, 14 English accents, scored with AppTek's own script), Rumble-2-Flash reaches 7.86% WER , on par with NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe (30B) at 7.78%. That's well ahead of Qwen3-ASR 0.6B (8.7%), from the same model family, and close to Qwen3-ASR 1.7B (7.4%), the only model in the comparison that does better. Real phone calls, 14 English accents Try it The weights are on the Hub at Reson8/Rumble-2-Flash . It's also available through our API . We're very curious what you'll build with it. Tell us in the Discussions tab what you've made, what you like, and what you'd like to see changed in a next version. items.raw_text: Back to Articles Rumble-2-Flash: an open 0.5B speech model for 40+ languages Published November 18, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 25 +19 Reson8 reson8-thomas Follow Reson8 Mark 't Hart MarktHart Follow Reson8 Eustache Le Bihan eustlb Follow Eric Bezzam bezzam Follow Today we're open sourcing Rumble-2-Flash under the Apache 2.0 license. It's a 0.5B-parameter speech recognition model for 40+ languages that competes with models 3-60x its size. Runs anywhere : native support in 🤗 Transformers and vLLM, no custom code 40+ languages : automatic language detection Output control : numbers as digits or words, fillers, verbatim repeats, forced language Extremely fast : an hour of audio in about half a second, with over 7,000 RTFx on full batches Holds up on real phone calls : on par with NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe (30B) on a 302-hour call-centre benchmark Quickstart Transcribe with 🤗 Transformers uv pip install torch transformers accelerate from transformers import AutoProcessor, AutoModelForMultimodalLM model_id = "Reson8/Rumble-2-Flash" processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id) model = AutoModelForMultimodalLM.from_pretrained(model_id, device_map= "auto" ) inputs = processor.apply_transcription_request( audio= "https://hf.co/datasets/hf-internal-testing/dummy-audio-samples/resolve/main/bcn_weather.mp3" , language= "English" , # omit to detect automatically ).to(model.device, dtype=model.dtype) output = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens= 512 ) generated = output[:, inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[- 1 ]:] print (processor.decode(generated, return_format= "transcription_only" )[ 0 ]) # return_format="parsed" if detecting language audio accepts a local path, a URL, a NumPy array, or a list of these. How it's built Rumble-2-Flash uses the Qwen3-ASR architecture for day-0 support. If your stack runs Transformers or vLLM, it runs Rumble-2-Flash, with no forked runtime or trust_remote_code . To find out how small a model could get before accuracy dropped off, we distilled Rumble-2, our larger production model, into it with on-policy distillation. The student doesn't train on transcripts the teacher wrote. It transcribes the audio itself, and the teacher grades that transcript token by token: at every position, it gives its own probability for what should come next, and the student learns to match it. Because the student learns from its own outputs, it gets corrected on exactly the mistakes it makes, with feedback on every token instead of one score per clip. On-policy distillation normally requires teacher and student to share a tokenizer, and ours don't: choosing Qwen3-ASR meant taking its vocabulary too. GOLD removes that restriction. It merges tokens where the two tokenizers split the text differently, so both models are compared over the same text. Tokens that exist in both vocabularies are compared directly, and the rest by their sorted probabilities. On-policy distillation with GOLD Results Accuracy for its size On the Open ASR Leaderboard multilingual track, Rumble-2-Flash averages a 6.96% error rate across Chinese, German, French, Italian, Spanish, Portuguese, Hindi, Dutch and English. That's better than Meta's omniASR-LLM 7B, a model 15x larger, and ahead of Whisper large-v3. On the English track it averages 6.6% WER . The best score for its size Speed Rumble-2-Flash is also fast. Its throughput depends on how full the batches are: on the larger datasets in HF's Open ASR Leaderboard, where batches stay full, it reaches over 7,000 RTFx . That's an hour of audio in about half a second. Real phone calls Clean audio is easy. Phone calls are compressed and noisy, and often have speakers with very different accents. On AppTek's call-centre benchmark (302 hours of helpline calls, 14 English accents, scored with AppTek's own script), Rumble-2-Flash reaches 7.86% WER , on par with NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe (30B) at 7.78%. That's well ahead of Qwen3-ASR 0.6B (8.7%), from the same model family, and close to Qwen3-ASR 1.7B (7.4%), the only model in the comparison that does better. Real phone calls, 14 English accents Try it The weights are on the Hub at Reson8/Rumble-2-Flash . It's also available through our API . We're very curious what you'll build with it.
