However, time pressure is a major determinant of human decision-making quality, and temporal state is a missing dimension of human behavioral modeling. This paper introduces a time-aware transformer that extends a Chessformer-style architecture with learned temporal conditioning tokens encoding player clock state, time control, and recent tempo, together with behavioral heads for thinking time and resignation. The model is trained on large-scale online chess data and evaluated against time-agnostic baselines and the state of the art. Results show that temporal conditioning yields modest overall accuracy improvements but substantially stronger gains under time pressure. Beyond move choice, it also produces more accurate thinking-time and resignation predictions. More importantly, the model better matches human move-quality degradation in critical time regimes, reducing the systematic over-strength observed in time-agnostic behavioral cloning models. These results suggest that temporal state is a previously underutilized but important signal for human behavioral cloning in chess. Index Terms: behavioral cloning, chess, transformers, temporal modeling, human-AI alignment I Introduction Most chess engines are built to play as strongly as possible. A different goal is to play like a human: reproducing the distribution of moves a player of a given strength would choose, including their mistakes. Such models power realistic sparring partners and bots. They also drive coaching tools that show a learner the kind of move a player at their level would make, and cheat-detection systems that flag games too strong to be human. From a player’s perspective, believability matters as much as raw accuracy, an opponent that feels human keeps players engaged, while one that plays robotically breaks the experience. The behavioral cloning paradigm in chess was first established by Maia [ 1 ] with per-rating convolutional networks, which were later unified into a single skill-conditioned model [ 2 ] ; Allie [ 3 ] moved to a text-based transformer over the move transcript, with search; and Maia-3 [ 4 ] , built on the Chessformer architecture, returned to a spatial representation, treating the 64 squares as tokens in an encoder-only transformer. However, each of them discards the clock. Remaining time does not condition the policy, so none of these models can learn how a human’s move choices shift as time runs out. Research on the speed–accuracy trade-off in chess shows that time restriction shifts the balance between recognition-based and calculation-based play, changing which moves a human is likely to choose [ 5 ] . Human decision quality falls sharply as the clock runs down, which we quantify in Section V-B . A model blind to the clock is forced to learn a single averaged policy that conflates comfortable and time-pressured play. This averaging is most damaging in critically time-pressured play, where human behavior diverges most. This paper addresses this gap with one claim: conditioning a strong chess policy on temporal state makes its behavior more human-like, with the effect concentrated under time pressure, where a time-blind model keeps playing too strongly precisely when humans play worst. Our contributions are: • input-level temporal conditioning for a chess transformer: clock state, time control, and recent tempo supplied as conditioning tokens the policy attends to; • a controlled, step-matched ablation at the 23M scale showing that the accuracy gain concentrates monotonically under time pressure and with player skill, and that the sampled policy reproduces the human move-quality degradation that a time-blind twin cannot express; • two intervention probes (counterfactual injection and permutation of the dynamic temporal inputs) that isolate the trained model’s dependence on the clock from its dependence on correlated position features; and • a graded comparison against the released Maia-3 model, from its own filtered evaluation regime to the full spectrum of human play. II Related Work Human behavioral cloning in chess. Maia [ 1 ] trained one convolutional network per rating band. Maia-2 [ 2 ] replaced these with a single architecture conditioned on a skill embedding, enabling smooth interpolation across ratings. Allie [ 3 ] reframed the problem as next-token prediction over game transcripts, gaining access to full history and predicting thinking time and resignation in addition to the move, with KL-regularized search at inference [ 6 ] . Maia-3 [ 4 ] represents the board directly, one token per square, with a geometric attention bias, achieving the strongest reported move-matching accuracy. Related work has also demonstrated grandmaster-level play from transformers without search [ 7 ] , a different objective from human alignment, and recent work extends Maia-3 toward individual style with rating-conditioned residual player embeddings [ 8 ] . Time as a signal. Large-scale analyses of online play have related human error to player skill, position difficulty, and the time available for a move [ 9 ] , yet existing models have handled the clock in one of three ways. The Maia line filters time pressure out: training data excludes all positions after the first time a player drops below 30 seconds remaining [ 1 , 4 ] , so the models never see the regime where the clock dominates behavior. Allie retains these positions and includes the static time control in its input, but predicts thinking time only as an output; its policy never observes the dynamic clock state, i.e., remaining time or recent tempo [ 3 ] . In recent work, UniMaia-Aux [ 10 ] modulates a frozen chess policy through natural-language prompts whose metadata can include remaining time and last-move delay, with auxiliary delay and resignation objectives. Overall, existing approaches either filter time pressure out or use clock information only indirectly, through auxiliary objectives or prompting rather than integrating dynamic temporal state directly into policy generation. III Method III-A Backbone We build on the Chessformer architecture [ 4 ] , the encoder-only backbone of the Maia-3 models, and leave it unchanged. Each of the 64 squares is a token whose features are dominated by the board itself: one-hot piece occupancy over the current and seven previous positions, to which a few auxiliary planes (en passant, castling rights, and repetition flags) and the skill embedding are appended as additional channels. Player and opponent skill are encoded by interpolating, independently per side, between two learned anchor embeddings at Elo 0 and 5000; the resulting vector is the same for every square and is concatenated into the per-square channels before a single input projection forms the tokens. Each encoder block applies a geometric attention bias that injects board geometry into attention, together with RMSNorm and a GELU feed-forward sub-layer. A bilinear from/to factorization over the 64 squares produces the policy, and a mean-pooled head predicts the win/draw/loss outcome. Our 23M configuration uses an embedding width of 512, 16 attention heads, and 8 blocks; the 79M configuration doubles the width to 1024 with 32 heads. Everything above is the Chessformer design unchanged; our additions, temporal conditioning and the behavioral heads, follow. items.content: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2611.33098 (cs) [Submitted on 24 Nov 2026] Title: Delegent: A Multi-Agent Harness That Reduces Cost without Sacrificing Performance Authors: Lingwei Gu , Jimmy Lin View a PDF of the paper titled Delegent: A Multi-Agent Harness That Reduces Cost without Sacrificing Performance, by Lingwei Gu and 1 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Agents built on frontier language models are expensive. At every step, the frontier model re-reads its entire context and executes every subtask regardless of its difficulty. This paper explores the simple thesis that much of this cost can be removed by delegating easy subtasks to a small language model, or SLM, that runs on hardware one already owns. To test it, we build Delegent, a simple and effective agent harness built on Claude Code, in which the frontier model stays in charge of every task but hands focused subtasks, such as investigating code, running tests, and searching a corpus, to SLM subagents. Existing approaches such as cascades and model routers usually choose which model executes the entire task, whereas in Delegent, the frontier model always leads the execution and delegates easy subtasks to the SLM. No router or model is trained, so either model can be swapped freely. With the help of a 27B FP8 SLM, Delegent reduces the frontier cost of long-horizon coding by 67% and of agentic search by 59%, with no loss in task performance, and even a 2B SLM that fits on a laptop reduces the coding cost by 66%. The savings grow with the legwork that the frontier model would otherwise do itself, and a short instruction, which leaves the main coding tasks to the frontier model, accounts for most of the saving and keeps the 2B SLM from losing tasks. items.content: Delegent: A Multi-Agent Harness That Reduces Cost without Sacrificing Performance Lingwei Gu Affiliation: David R. Cheriton School of Computer Science Jimmy Lin Affiliation: University of Waterloo Abstract Agents built on frontier language models are expensive. At every step, the frontier model re-reads its entire context and executes every subtask regardless of its difficulty. This paper explores the simple thesis that much of this cost can be removed by delegating easy subtasks to a small language model, or SLM, that runs on hardware one already owns. To test it, we build Delegent, a simple and effective agent harness built on Claude Code, in which the frontier model stays in charge of every task but hands focused subtasks, such as investigating code, running tests, and searching a corpus, to SLM subagents. Existing approaches such as cascades and model routers usually choose which model executes the entire task, whereas in Delegent, the frontier model always leads the execution and delegates easy subtasks to the SLM. No router or model is trained, so either model can be swapped freely. With the help of a 27B FP8 SLM, Delegent reduces the frontier cost of long-horizon coding by 67% and of agentic search by 59%, with no loss in task performance, and even a 2B SLM that fits on a laptop reduces the coding cost by 66%. The savings grow with the legwork that the frontier model would otherwise do itself, and a short instruction, which leaves the main coding tasks to the frontier model, accounts for most of the saving and keeps the 2B SLM from losing tasks. Code: https://github.com/castorini/delegent . Main loop Frontier model Subagents SLM spawn Agent Delegate get_document search Bash Read Edit … visit Environment repository or corpus User task answer Figure 1: The Delegent harness. It starts from the stock Claude Code harness, and everything in orange is what we add. The user talks to the main loop, where the frontier model leads the task and spawns subagents. The loops share most tools, and each adds a few. 1 Introduction Agents are simply models using tools in loops. The harness invokes the model, executes its tool calls, returns the results, and invokes the model again, until the task is done. The loop is simple but costly, because at every step the model re-reads its entire context, which grows with every tool call. A frontier coding agent that takes a hundred steps to resolve an issue thus pays for a hundred ever longer prompts. Long-horizon agents are therefore expensive for organizations that pay per token, and individuals on subscription plans exhaust their quota and have to wait for the next reset. Yet much of what a frontier model does at each step is easy legwork, such as locating the relevant code, reproducing a bug, running tests, issuing searches, and reading documents. Little of this work seems to require a frontier model, yet existing agents use the frontier model for all of it, even in subagents, billing every step at frontier prices. A small language model, or SLM, costs far less, and nothing extra on a GPU that one already owns. An SLM on its own falls well short of a frontier model on these tasks and cannot replace one, but it does not need to compete with the frontier if the frontier model stays in charge and delegates only easy subtasks. This leads to a simple thesis: A small language model running on local hardware can take over the easy subtasks of a frontier model, cutting its cost substantially without hurting task performance, and without any training. To test this thesis, we build Delegent ( Figure 1 ), an agent harness that runs a frontier model and a local SLM as a team. For coding, Delegent is derived from Claude Code. 1 1 1 https://code.claude.com/docs It keeps the agent loop and subagents of Claude Code, but routes each model call by role, sending the calls of the main loop to the frontier model and the calls of its subagents to the SLM. For agentic search, it adds a Delegate tool whose subagents search the corpus and return reports with evidence. The frontier model stays in charge of every task. A short instruction tells it what to delegate, the harness runs the delegated subtasks on the SLM and checks the evidence in their reports, and the frontier model alone produces the final answer. Since nothing is trained, either model is a drop-in component. As the headline result, we find that the thesis holds on both long-horizon coding and agentic search. With GPT-6.1-Sol at high reasoning effort as the frontier model and Qwen3.8-27B-FP8 as the SLM, the frontier model’s cost on DeepSWE falls to a third, with no loss in resolved tasks. On 694 search questions, its cost falls to 41%, and it answers exactly as many questions correctly as on its own. Even a 2B model, MiniCPM5-2B, cuts frontier cost on DeepSWE to a third, and with Qwen3.8-27B-FP8 paid for at API prices, the total cost of a DeepSWE task is still only 38%. Delegation adds some latency, which is bounded by the local hardware that serves the SLM. Contrary to the dominant approach to combining cheap and expensive models, we do not let the SLM answer first and then decide whether to trust it ( Chen et al., 2024 ; Aggarwal et al., 2024 ; Yue et al., 2024 ) , nor do we train a router that picks one model per query ( Ding et al., 2024 ; Ong et al., 2025 ) . In both cases, a model is given the entire task and must solve it by itself, which a 2B SLM is rarely capable of. In Delegent, the frontier model always produces the final answer, and the SLM only does the legwork. No output of the SLM is accepted without the frontier model reading it first. Our contribution is thus a piece of harness engineering: the coordination of two models of very different cost. To better circumscribe our claims, let us be more precise: • By cost , we mean what the frontier model is charged, with prompt caching taken into account. The SLM runs on a GPU under the user’s control, and for coding, we also price Qwen3.8-27B-FP8 at API prices. • By local , we mean an SLM served on a single GPU under the user’s control. The 27B FP8 model needs a workstation GPU, and the 2B model fits on a laptop. • By training-free , we mean that no model is trained or fine-tuned, so the SLM and the frontier model can each be swapped freely. This paper makes three contributions. First, we build Delegent, an open-source, training-free harness in which a frontier model delegates work to a local SLM, which we describe in Section 2 . Second, we evaluate it on three coding and five search datasets with two SLMs of very different sizes, and show in Section 4 that frontier cost falls by more than half in eight of nine evaluations while task performance holds. Third, we analyze in Section 5 where the savings come from and how they depend on our instruction and the frontier model. 2 The Delegent Harness Delegent is built on Claude Code and coordinates two models of very different cost, as Figure 1 illustrates. The frontier model leads every task. It plans, decides what to delegate and whether to believe what comes back, and writes the final patch or answer. SLM subagents on a local GPU do the legwork, each in its own tool loop and with a fresh context. Delegent lets the frontier model judge the task type, coding or search, and supplies the matching tool set. Routing model calls by role. In Claude Code, the main loop calls a model at every step, and so does each subagent that it starts with the built-in Agent tool. Minor jobs go to a small auxiliary model. For each task, Delegent places a relay between Claude Code and the models. The relay speaks the Anthropic Messages API, so Claude Code runs unmodified, and it routes each call according to the model that the call names. Calls from the main loop go to the frontier model, and calls from the subagents and the auxiliary model go to the SLM. Every frontier call within a task carries the same prompt-cache key, so consecutive steps hit the provider’s cache. SLM calls go to vLLM ( Kwon et al., 2023 ) through a proxy that pins each subagent to one GPU replica, so its growing prefix stays cached. Running subtasks. For coding, the frontier model delegates a subtask through its Agent tool and writes a brief, the instructions for the Claude Code subagent. The subagent works in the same container with Claude Code’s default tools. For search, Delegent adds a Delegate tool for delegating one focused search subtask, such as finding or checking a fact. Instead of designing the search subagent from scratch, we borrow from AREX ( Lu et al., 2026 ) , a family of deep research agents. Its smallest member, AREX-Turbo, is built around a 4B model, so its prompts and tools are already written for a small model to follow. An AREX-Turbo agent works in a loop with four tools: it searches the corpus, visits the documents it finds, compresses its own history into notes when the history grows long, and finishes with an answer, the evidence that supports it, and a confidence. Our SLM subagent sees only the subtask and the question, and its final answer, evidence, and confidence form the report that returns to the frontier model. In both coding and search, subtasks from one turn run concurrently. Returning reports. The frontier model’s context receives only the final report of a subagent and none of its tool outputs. For search, the harness also looks up each evidence line in the cited document and notes whether it was found verbatim. Steering the frontier model. A short instruction ( Appendix A ) explains the economics to the frontier model. Since every step re-reads the entire context, the cheapest plan has the fewest steps of the frontier model’s own, so the instruction asks it to delegate tool-heavy work and to keep its own tool use to a few targeted checks. It covers both kinds of delegation, Claude Code’s subagents for coding and the Delegate tool for search. 3 Experimental Setup Tasks. For coding, we use random samples of SWE-bench Verified ( Jimenez et al., 2024 ) , 2 2 2 https://openai.com/index/introducing-swe-bench-verified/ SWE-bench Pro ( Deng et al., 2025 ) , and DeepSWE v1.1 ( Huang et al., 2026 ) , drawn as described in Appendix C . For search, we use 200 BrowseComp-Plus questions ( Chen et al., 2025 ) , randomly sampled from those not used to draft the instruction, and four datasets from CMASS ( Sharifymoghaddam et al., 2026 ) , an agentic search benchmark over ClimbMix ( Diao et al., 2025 ) , an open web corpus of 400B tokens that agents can access only through BM25 search ( Robertson and Zaragoza, 2009 ; Lin et al., 2021 ) . The CMASS datasets are BrowseComp-Plus, Total Recall QA ( Rafiee et al., 2026 ) , HotpotQA ( Yang et al., 2018 ) , and DeepSearchQA ( Gupta et al., 2026 ) , which we abbreviate as TRQA and DSQA. DSQA questions have several correct answers, and CMASS evaluates them in two modes. In find one , any correct answer counts, while find all needs the exact set. Models. All our runs use the Delegent harness, built on Claude Code, and the frontier model it calls can change freely. Our main experiments call GPT-6.1-Sol , accessed through the OpenAI API, and on DeepSWE we run ablations with Claude Opus 5.5 at xhigh effort. We run Sol at high reasoning effort, the same with and without delegation, to keep our experiments affordable. At this effort, it resolves just over half of the DeepSWE tasks alone. We pair it with two SLMs of very different sizes, both easy to run on a single device. Qwen3.8-27B-FP8 3 3 3 https://qwen.ai/blog?id=qwen3.8 fits on one workstation GPU, and MiniCPM5-2B ( Hu et al., 2024 ; MiniCPM Team, 2025 ) is small enough for a laptop. We serve both with vLLM, one GPU per replica, and test MiniCPM5-2B on coding only. Baseline. We compare against the frontier model alone on the same tasks, using the same harness without the delegation tool and instruction. For coding, this is Claude Code with its default tools and subagents, where we send every call to the frontier model, including the calls that Claude Code sends to Haiku by default. As a sanity check, Claude Opus 5.5 alone resolves 68% of our DeepSWE tasks in this setup, in line with the 68.4% that Artificial Analysis reports for Claude Opus 5.5 in Claude Code. 4 4 4 https://x.com/ArtificialAnlys/status/2102932119995756613 , for Claude Opus 5.5 at max effort on DeepSWE v1.1. Metrics. A coding task is resolved if the final patch passes the task’s hidden tests. A search answer is graded against the gold answer by GPT-6.1-Sol at low effort with the official BrowseComp-Plus grading prompt ( Chen et al., 2025 ) , and the same judge grades every system. All coding runs, including those of the frontier model alone, use Claude Code with its default tools except web access, a context of up to 1M tokens for the frontier model and 131k tokens for the SLM, and the same limits on turns and time, which Appendix B lists. Latency is wall-clock time per task. Cost. We count frontier cost at the API prices of the frontier model, 5 5 5 https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/pricing , accessed October 2026. with prompt caching for every system : cost = $ 2 T in uncached + $ 0.10 T in cached + $ 10 T out , \text{cost}=\$2\,T_{\text{in}}^{\text{uncached}}+\$0.10\,T_{\text{in}}^{\text{cached}}+\$10\,T_{\text{out}}, where T T are token counts in millions and output includes reasoning tokens. We report cost per task and relative to the frontier model alone. For coding, we also price Qwen3.8-27B-FP8 at the API rates of Chutes, a provider that serves the same FP8 model, with prompt caching as well. items.raw_text: Delegent: A Multi-Agent Harness That Reduces Cost without Sacrificing Performance Lingwei Gu Affiliation: David R. Cheriton School of Computer Science Jimmy Lin Affiliation: University of Waterloo Abstract Agents built on frontier language models are expensive. At every step, the frontier model re-reads its entire context and executes every subtask regardless of its difficulty. This paper explores the simple thesis that much of this cost can be removed by delegating easy subtasks to a small language model, or SLM, that runs on hardware one already owns. To test it, we build Delegent, a simple and effective agent harness built on Claude Code, in which the frontier model stays in charge of every task but hands focused subtasks, such as investigating code, running tests, and searching a corpus, to SLM subagents. Existing approaches such as cascades and model routers usually choose which model executes the entire task, whereas in Delegent, the frontier model always leads the execution and delegates easy subtasks to the SLM. No router or model is trained, so either model can be swapped freely. With the help of a 27B FP8 SLM, Delegent reduces the frontier cost of long-horizon coding by 67% and of agentic search by 59%, with no loss in task performance, and even a 2B SLM that fits on a laptop reduces the coding cost by 66%. The savings grow with the legwork that the frontier model would otherwise do itself, and a short instruction, which leaves the main coding tasks to the frontier model, accounts for most of the saving and keeps the 2B SLM from losing tasks. Code: https://github.com/castorini/delegent . Main loop Frontier model Subagents SLM spawn Agent Delegate get_document search Bash Read Edit … visit Environment repository or corpus User task answer Figure 1: The Delegent harness. It starts from the stock Claude Code harness, and everything in orange is what we add. The user talks to the main loop, where the frontier model leads the task and spawns subagents. The loops share most tools, and each adds a few. 1 Introduction Agents are simply models using tools in loops. The harness invokes the model, executes its tool calls, returns the results, and invokes the model again, until the task is done. The loop is simple but costly, because at every step the model re-reads its entire context, which grows with every tool call. A frontier coding agent that takes a hundred steps to resolve an issue thus pays for a hundred ever longer prompts. Long-horizon agents are therefore expensive for organizations that pay per token, and individuals on subscription plans exhaust their quota and have to wait for the next reset. Yet much of what a frontier model does at each step is easy legwork, such as locating the relevant code, reproducing a bug, running tests, issuing searches, and reading documents. Little of this work seems to require a frontier model, yet existing agents use the frontier model for all of it, even in subagents, billing every step at frontier prices. A small language model, or SLM, costs far less, and nothing extra on a GPU that one already owns. An SLM on its own falls well short of a frontier model on these tasks and cannot replace one, but it does not need to compete with the frontier if the frontier model stays in charge and delegates only easy subtasks. This leads to a simple thesis: A small language model running on local hardware can take over the easy subtasks of a frontier model, cutting its cost substantially without hurting task performance, and without any training. To test this thesis, we build Delegent ( Figure 1 ), an agent harness that runs a frontier model and a local SLM as a team. For coding, Delegent is derived from Claude Code. 1 1 1 https://code.claude.com/docs It keeps the agent loop and subagents of Claude Code, but routes each model call by role, sending the calls of the main loop to the frontier model and the calls of its subagents to the SLM. For agentic search, it adds a Delegate tool whose subagents search the corpus and return reports with evidence. The frontier model stays in charge of every task. A short instruction tells it what to delegate, the harness runs the delegated subtasks on the SLM and checks the evidence in their reports, and the frontier model alone produces the final answer. Since nothing is trained, either model is a drop-in component. As the headline result, we find that the thesis holds on both long-horizon coding and agentic search. With GPT-6.1-Sol at high reasoning effort as the frontier model and Qwen3.8-27B-FP8 as the SLM, the frontier model’s cost on DeepSWE falls to a third, with no loss in resolved tasks. On 694 search questions, its cost falls to 41%, and it answers exactly as many questions correctly as on its own. Even a 2B model, MiniCPM5-2B, cuts frontier cost on DeepSWE to a third, and with Qwen3.8-27B-FP8 paid for at API prices, the total cost of a DeepSWE task is still only 38%. Delegation adds some latency, which is bounded by the local hardware that serves the SLM. Contrary to the dominant approach to combining cheap and expensive models, we do not let the SLM answer first and then decide whether to trust it ( Chen et al., 2024 ; Aggarwal et al., 2024 ; Yue et al., 2024 ) , nor do we train a router that picks one model per query ( Ding et al., 2024 ; Ong et al., 2025 ) . In both cases, a model is given the entire task and must solve it by itself, which a 2B SLM is rarely capable of. In Delegent, the frontier model always produces the final answer, and the SLM only does the legwork. No output of the SLM is accepted without the frontier model reading it first. Our contribution is thus a piece of harness engineering: the coordination of two models of very different cost. To better circumscribe our claims, let us be more precise: • By cost , we mean what the frontier model is charged, with prompt caching taken into account. The SLM runs on a GPU under the user’s control, and for coding, we also price Qwen3.8-27B-FP8 at API prices. • By local , we mean an SLM served on a single GPU under the user’s control. The 27B FP8 model needs a workstation GPU, and the 2B model fits on a laptop. • By training-free , we mean that no model is trained or fine-tuned, so the SLM and the frontier model can each be swapped freely. This paper makes three contributions. First, we build Delegent, an open-source, training-free harness in which a frontier model delegates work to a local SLM, which we describe in Section 2 . Second, we evaluate it on three coding and five search datasets with two SLMs of very different sizes, and show in Section 4 that frontier cost falls by more than half in eight of nine evaluations while task performance holds. Third, we analyze in Section 5 where the savings come from and how they depend on our instruction and the frontier model. 2 The Delegent Harness Delegent is built on Claude Code and coordinates two models of very different cost, as Figure 1 illustrates. The frontier model leads every task. It plans, decides what to delegate and whether to believe what comes back, and writes the final patch or answer. SLM subagents on a local GPU do the legwork, each in its own tool loop and with a fresh context. Delegent lets the frontier model judge the task type, coding or search, and supplies the matching tool set. Routing model calls by role. In Claude Code, the main loop calls a model at every step, and so does each subagent that it starts with the built-in Agent tool. Minor jobs go to a small auxiliary model. For each task, Delegent places a relay between Claude Code and the models. The relay speaks the Anthropic Messages API, so Claude Code runs unmodified, and it routes each call according to the model that the call names. Calls from the main loop go to the frontier model, and calls from the subagents and the auxiliary model go to the SLM. Every frontier call within a task carries the same prompt-cache key, so consecutive steps hit the provider’s cache. SLM calls go to vLLM ( Kwon et al., 2023 ) through a proxy that pins each subagent to one GPU replica, so its growing prefix stays cached. Running subtasks. For coding, the frontier model delegates a subtask through its Agent tool and writes a brief, the instructions for the Claude Code subagent. The subagent works in the same container with Claude Code’s default tools. For search, Delegent adds a Delegate tool for delegating one focused search subtask, such as finding or checking a fact. Instead of designing the search subagent from scratch, we borrow from AREX ( Lu et al., 2026 ) , a family of deep research agents. Its smallest member, AREX-Turbo, is built around a 4B model, so its prompts and tools are already written for a small model to follow. An AREX-Turbo agent works in a loop with four tools: it searches the corpus, visits the documents it finds, compresses its own history into notes when the history grows long, and finishes with an answer, the evidence that supports it, and a confidence. Our SLM subagent sees only the subtask and the question, and its final answer, evidence, and confidence form the report that returns to the frontier model. In both coding and search, subtasks from one turn run concurrently. Returning reports. The frontier model’s context receives only the final report of a subagent and none of its tool outputs. For search, the harness also looks up each evidence line in the cited document and notes whether it was found verbatim. Steering the frontier model. A short instruction ( Appendix A ) explains the economics to the frontier model. Since every step re-reads the entire context, the cheapest plan has the fewest steps of the frontier model’s own, so the instruction asks it to delegate tool-heavy work and to keep its own tool use to a few targeted checks. It covers both kinds of delegation, Claude Code’s subagents for coding and the Delegate tool for search. 3 Experimental Setup Tasks. For coding, we use random samples of SWE-bench Verified ( Jimenez et al., 2024 ) , 2 2 2 https://openai.com/index/introducing-swe-bench-verified/ SWE-bench Pro ( Deng et al., 2025 ) , and DeepSWE v1.1 ( Huang et al., 2026 ) , drawn as described in Appendix C . For search, we use 200 BrowseComp-Plus questions ( Chen et al., 2025 ) , randomly sampled from those not used to draft the instruction, and four datasets from CMASS ( Sharifymoghaddam et al., 2026 ) , an agentic search benchmark over ClimbMix ( Diao et al., 2025 ) , an open web corpus of 400B tokens that agents can access only through BM25 search ( Robertson and Zaragoza, 2009 ; Lin et al., 2021 ) . The CMASS datasets are BrowseComp-Plus, Total Recall QA ( Rafiee et al., 2026 ) , HotpotQA ( Yang et al., 2018 ) , and DeepSearchQA ( Gupta et al., 2026 ) , which we abbreviate as TRQA and DSQA. DSQA questions have several correct answers, and CMASS evaluates them in two modes. In find one , any correct answer counts, while find all needs the exact set. Models. All our runs use the Delegent harness, built on Claude Code, and the frontier model it calls can change freely. Our main experiments call GPT-6.1-Sol , accessed through the OpenAI API, and on DeepSWE we run ablations with Claude Opus 5.5 at xhigh effort. We run Sol at high reasoning effort, the same with and without delegation, to keep our experiments affordable. At this effort, it resolves just over half of the DeepSWE tasks alone. We pair it with two SLMs of very different sizes, both easy to run on a single device. Qwen3.8-27B-FP8 3 3 3 https://qwen.ai/blog?id=qwen3.8 fits on one workstation GPU, and MiniCPM5-2B ( Hu et al., 2024 ; MiniCPM Team, 2025 ) is small enough for a laptop. We serve both with vLLM, one GPU per replica, and test MiniCPM5-2B on coding only. Baseline. We compare against the frontier model alone on the same tasks, using the same harness without the delegation tool and instruction. For coding, this is Claude Code with its default tools and subagents, where we send every call to the frontier model, including the calls that Claude Code sends to Haiku by default. A search answer is graded against the gold answer by GPT-6.1-Sol at low effort with the official BrowseComp-Plus grading prompt ( Chen et al., 2025 ) , and the same judge grades every system. All coding runs, including those of the frontier model alone, use Claude Code with its default tools except web access, a context of up to 1M tokens for the frontier model and 131k tokens for the SLM, and the same limits on turns and time, which Appendix B lists. items.content: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2611.33086 (cs) [Submitted on 24 Nov 2026] Title: Uncertainty-Aware Candidate Generation for Entity Linking in Cyber Threat Intelligence Authors: Nasser Alkhulaifi , Direnc Pekaslan , Christian Wagner View a PDF of the paper titled Uncertainty-Aware Candidate Generation for Entity Linking in Cyber Threat Intelligence, by Nasser Alkhulaifi and Direnc Pekaslan and Christian Wagner View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Entity Resolution (ER) pipelines often collapse ambiguity into early hard decisions: upstream Named Entity Recognition (NER) selects a single span and type, and downstream Entity Linking (EL) treats that choice as ground truth. This discards valuable information about the ambiguity of the underlying data (e.g., span boundary disagreement and type confusion), leading to brittle systems that fail unpredictably when faced with uncertainty in inputs. Therefore, this work presents a proof-of-concept for uncertainty-aware ER that treats uncertainty as native data that should be preserved and exploited throughout ER pipelines. We (i) capture uncertainty signals in the NER stage and (ii) leverage these signals into the EL stage to improve candidate retrieval under ambiguity. Using a BERT-based NER model augmented with two auxiliary span-boundary prediction heads, we apply Monte Carlo (MC) dropout at inference time to derive three mention-level proxy signals: the MC-averaged start-boundary probability, the MC-averaged end-boundary probability, and De Luca-Termini fuzzy entropy computed over the Begin-Inside-Outside (BIO) predictive distribution. These signals are used to adapt the fuzzy cutoff in candidate generation (CG) for EL. Because CG is treated as a blocking step, we evaluate retrieval recall. On the AnnoCTR dataset linked to the MITRE ATTCK knowledge base, the boundary-aware and dual-signal fuzzy linking approaches improve Recall@10 from 0.6186 to 0.7966. The contribution lies not in an end-to-end optimised ER pipeline but in establishing uncertainty preservation as a viable and beneficial component of ER pipelines, enabling downstream EL to make better-informed decisions under uncertainty. items.content: Uncertainty-Aware Candidate Generation for Entity Linking in Cyber Threat Intelligence Nasser Alkhulaifi 1,2 , Direnc Pekaslan 1 and Christian Wagner 1 1 LUCID Lab, School of Computer Science, University of Nottingham, Nottingham, UK 2 COL Lab, School of Computer Science, University of Nottingham, UK { Nasser.Alkhulaifi,Direnc.Pekaslan1,Christian.Wagner } @nottingham.ac.uk Abstract Entity Resolution (ER) pipelines often collapse ambiguity into early hard decisions: upstream Named Entity Recognition (NER) selects a single span and type, and downstream Entity Linking (EL) treats that choice as ground truth. This discards valuable information about the ambiguity of the underlying data (e.g., span boundary disagreement and type confusion), leading to brittle systems that fail unpredictably when faced with uncertainty in inputs. Therefore, this work presents a proof-of-concept for uncertainty-aware ER that treats uncertainty as native data that should be preserved and exploited throughout ER pipelines. We (i) capture uncertainty signals in the NER stage and (ii) leverage these signals into the EL stage to improve candidate retrieval under ambiguity. Using a BERT-based NER model augmented with two auxiliary span-boundary prediction heads, we apply Monte Carlo (MC) dropout at inference time to derive three mention-level proxy signals: the MC-averaged start-boundary probability, the MC-averaged end-boundary probability, and De Luca–Termini fuzzy entropy computed over the Begin–Inside–Outside (BIO) predictive distribution. These signals are used to adapt the fuzzy cutoff in candidate generation (CG) for EL. Because CG is treated as a blocking step, we evaluate retrieval recall. On the AnnoCTR dataset linked to the MITRE ATT&CK knowledge base, the boundary-aware and dual-signal fuzzy linking approaches improve Recall@10 from 0.6186 to 0.7966. The contribution lies not in an end-to-end optimised ER pipeline but in establishing uncertainty preservation as a viable and beneficial component of ER pipelines, enabling downstream EL to make better-informed decisions under uncertainty. 1 Introduction and Background Entity Resolution (ER) aims to determine when different textual mentions or records refer to the same real-world entity and to align them to a canonical representation, typically within or across Knowledge Bases (KBs) [ 40 , 3 ] . Accurate ER is a prerequisite for the construction and maintenance of high-quality Knowledge Graphs (KGs), since unresolved duplicates and incorrect merges propagate errors to downstream analytics, search, and reasoning [ 36 , 41 ] . ER for unstructured text is commonly operationalised as a pipeline: entities are first detected and typed via Named Entity Recognition (NER), then grounded (linked) to a KB via Entity Linking (EL), enabling richer structured context for subsequent retrieval and inference [ 3 ] . The upstream task of ER is NER, a natural language processing (NLP) task that involves identifying specific mentions in a given text and classifying them into predefined entity types, such as location, organisation, or person [ 18 , 27 ] . NER is a well-studied problem in the literature, with early approaches relying on rules, dictionaries, and statistical taggers [ 25 ] , whereas modern approaches predominantly use deep-learning-based methods [ 20 ] . Recent progress is driven by contextual encoders, particularly Transformer-based models [ 5 , 34 , 16 ] . Among these methods, span-based NER has become more prevalent because, unlike token-level sequence tagging, it identifies entities by scoring spans directly [ 37 , 38 ] . Spans are often represented using features derived from the contextual embeddings of their boundary tokens (first and last) [ 33 ] , typically produced by a pretrained language model (e.g., BERT [ 5 ] or RoBERTa [ 22 ] ). This span-level modelling tends to improve robustness to out-of-vocabulary words [ 8 ] and to missing or unlabelled entities arising from annotation errors [ 21 ] . The downstream task following NER in an ER pipeline is EL, which takes the detected entity mentions and maps each one to its corresponding entity in a KB, bridging unstructured language with structured knowledge for retrieval and reasoning [ 3 ] . EL is commonly implemented as a two-stage process: (i) candidate generation (CG), also known as blocking, which retrieves a set of plausible KB entities using the mention while reducing the number of candidate descriptions to be compared, and (ii) entity matching, which ranks these candidates to resolve ambiguity using a set of functions (e.g., description similarity) [ 26 ] . Recent neural EL systems attempt to reduce reliance on hand-crafted similarity features by learning dense mention–context and entity representations (often using attention encoders) [ 28 ] . However, they typically remain challenged by long-tailed entity distributions (i.e., a few entities occur very frequently while many others are rare) and KB incompleteness (including NIL/unlinkable mentions), and can be computationally expensive, especially when using cross-encoder scoring for candidate ranking [ 30 , 36 , 28 ] . Many ER systems still couple NER and EL through point decisions: EL CG is conditioned on the single best NER span and type, rather than a calibrated uncertainty signal over alternative spans/types [ 17 , 35 ] . This design is brittle because mention resolution is often underdetermined: small boundary differences change the mention string used for alias lookup and string matching during CG, and type errors can exclude otherwise plausible candidates when type constraints are applied [ 35 , 29 , 10 ] . The result is error propagation: early ambiguity becomes a hard commitment that downstream linking cannot easily recover from [ 17 ] . Uncertainty arises at multiple stages in the ER pipeline, and is therefore a meaningful signal, not just noise. At the NER stage, uncertainty typically appears as (i) boundary uncertainty (where the mention starts/ends) and (ii) label uncertainty (which entity type applies); recent works have explored uncertainty estimation and calibration for sequence labelling and NER [ 11 , 12 , 14 , 39 ] . At the EL stage, uncertainty is driven by the knowledge base and data distribution itself: aliases are shared across entities, descriptions can be sparse, many entities are rare and therefore poorly represented, and some mentions are simply unlinkable (NIL) [ 13 , 10 , 29 ] . In practice, CG involves balancing high recall against the introduction of irrelevant candidates through choices such as exact versus fuzzy matching, similarity thresholds, and pruning rules [ 29 ] . When upstream evidence is weak, however, a fixed CG strategy can either miss the gold entity or admit too many irrelevant candidates [ 10 ] . Uncertainty estimation for neural NLP has been widely studied, with Monte Carlo (MC) dropout providing a standard approximate Bayesian approach [ 9 ] . For structured prediction, recent works target calibrated confidence and uncertainty scoring for outputs relevant to NER [ 11 , 12 , 14 ] . However, comparatively little work uses NER uncertainty as an explicit control signal to adapt the EL CG policy, despite evidence that NER decisions materially affect downstream linking [ 35 ] . Therefore, this work addresses that gap with an uncertainty-preserving design. We (i) extract mention-level uncertainty signals from a BERT-based NER model under MC dropout (boundary confidence and entropy) and (ii) leverage them to improve CG in EL. By preserving these uncertainty signals rather than reducing NER outputs to a single point estimate, the downstream EL stage is better able to support informed decision-making under uncertainty. For example, candidate-retrieval behaviour can be adapted when boundary confidence is low or entity-type entropy is high, thereby enabling more appropriate downstream decisions such as linking, abstaining from linking, or flagging the mention for further review instead of forcing an early commitment to an uncertain match. The contributions of this work are summarised as follows: 1 1 1 The experimental code and materials required to reproduce the results are publicly available at: https://github.com/Nasser-Alkhulaifi/uncertainty-aware-cti-linking . • Extraction of uncertainty signals at the NER stage by augmenting the model with two auxiliary span-boundary prediction heads (start/end), followed by MC dropout to estimate predictive uncertainty. • Use of these proxies to adapt EL CG and improve gold-entity retention in a cyber threat intelligence setting (i.e., support better-informed downstream decisions under uncertainty). The structure of the remaining sections of this paper is as follows: Section 2 describes how uncertainty signals are captured and leveraged, Section 3 details the datasets, experimental setup, and evaluation metric, Section 4 analyses and discusses the results, and Section 5 summarises the key findings, limitations, and directions for future work. Figure 1: Overview of our uncertainty-aware NER-to-EL approach: (i) capture and extract uncertainty signals in the NER stage and (ii) leverage these signals into the candidate retrieval stage to enable more robust and transparent linking decisions. The three captured uncertainty signals are (1) the MC-averaged start boundary probability, (2) the MC-averaged end boundary probability, and (3) the mention-level De Luca–Termini entropy over the normalised possibilistic span distribution. See Section 2 for more details on this approach and Section 3 for the experimental procedure. 2 Methods This section describes how uncertainty signals are extracted and leveraged across the NER-to-EL components of the text-oriented ER workflow, as shown in Figure 1 . Section 2.1 explains how uncertainty signals are captured at the NER level using a BERT-based approach augmented with MC dropout to estimate predictive uncertainty over entity spans and types. Section 2.2 explains how these signals are leveraged to retrieve candidates at the EL stage. 2.1 Capturing Uncertainty Signals To capture uncertainty at the NER stage, a BERT-based model was used to produce contextual token representations and decode them with a Begin–Inside–Outside (BIO) tagging head [ 42 ] , plus two auxiliary boundary heads (start/end). This separates token type assignment from boundary localisation: the BIO head uses softmax because BIO labels are mutually exclusive, while the boundary heads use sigmoid because start/end are independent token-wise binary events (and can both be true for single-token mentions). BIO decoding remains the primary extraction mechanism; boundary heads provide additional boundary-confidence signals. For uncertainty estimation, we apply MC dropout [ 9 , 31 ] at inference time and run M M stochastic passes. For BIO labels, we use the MC predictive distribution: p ¯ t ​ ( c ) = 1 M ​ ∑ m = 1 M softmax ​ ( z t , m ) c \bar{p}_{t}(c)=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{m=1}^{M}\mathrm{softmax}(z_{t,m})_{c} (1) where t t indexes tokens, m m indexes MC dropout passes, c c is a BIO class, z t , m z_{t,m} are the BIO logits at token t t in pass m m , and softmax ​ ( z t , m ) c \mathrm{softmax}(z_{t,m})_{c} denotes the predicted probability of class c c under that pass. q ¯ t s ​ t ​ a ​ r ​ t = 1 M ​ ∑ m = 1 M q t , m s ​ t ​ a ​ r ​ t \bar{q}^{start}_{t}=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{m=1}^{M}q^{start}_{t,m} (2) where q t , m s ​ t ​ a ​ r ​ t ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] q^{start}_{t,m}\in[0,1] is the sigmoid output for the start-boundary head at token t t in pass m m , and q ¯ t s ​ t ​ a ​ r ​ t \bar{q}^{start}_{t} is its MC-averaged start-boundary probability. q ¯ t e ​ n ​ d = 1 M ​ ∑ m = 1 M q t , m e ​ n ​ d \bar{q}^{end}_{t}=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{m=1}^{M}q^{end}_{t,m} (3) where q t , m e ​ n ​ d ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] q^{end}_{t,m}\in[0,1] is the sigmoid output for the end-boundary head at token t t in pass m m , and q ¯ t e ​ n ​ d \bar{q}^{end}_{t} is its MC-averaged end-boundary probability. Hence, the three captured signals are: (1) MC-averaged start-boundary probability q ¯ t s ​ t ​ a ​ r ​ t \bar{q}^{start}_{t} , (2) MC-averaged end-boundary probability q ¯ t e ​ n ​ d \bar{q}^{end}_{t} , and (3) mention-level De Luca--Termini entropy 2 2 2 De Luca & Termini entropy [ 4 ] on possibilistic distribution; measures average fuzziness of classification across span tokens; calculated after normalising probabilities to possibilities. , computed from the normalised possibilistic form of p ¯ t ​ ( c ) \bar{p}_{t}(c) and averaged across tokens in the predicted mention span. Together, these signals capture complementary uncertainty about boundary reliability and entity-type ambiguity, and are passed to the downstream EL stage. It is worth clarifying that, in this work, uncertainty refers to the instability of the NER model’s span and type predictions across repeated MC-dropout inference passes. By keeping dropout active at inference and running multiple stochastic forward passes, we approximate an ensemble of closely related models and observe how consistently these runs agree on BIO labels and on the start/end boundary estimates produced by the two auxiliary span-boundary prediction heads. Accordingly, the uncertainty considered here is upstream NER uncertainty about where a mention begins and ends and which entity type it should receive. It is not a direct confidence score for the final EL decision; for example, we do not estimate quantities such as this mention links to ATT&CK entity e e with probability p p . Nor do we propagate a full distribution over alternative spans or entity types into EL. Instead, we average the variability in the NER outputs using the three aforementioned mention-level proxy signals derived from the MC predictive BIO distribution over the predicted span tokens. These signals are used as heuristics for span reliability and type ambiguity: the boundary probabilities indicate confidence in the chosen start and end tokens, whereas the entropy score is a relative measure of type ambiguity, with higher values indicating greater ambiguity rather than a calibrated probability. 2.2 Leveraging Uncertainty Signals After uncertainty proxies have been derived at the NER stage, the EL candidate generator receives each predicted mention together with its boundary-confidence, entropy, and predicted-type information. items.raw_text: Uncertainty-Aware Candidate Generation for Entity Linking in Cyber Threat Intelligence Nasser Alkhulaifi 1,2 , Direnc Pekaslan 1 and Christian Wagner 1 1 LUCID Lab, School of Computer Science, University of Nottingham, Nottingham, UK 2 COL Lab, School of Computer Science, University of Nottingham, UK { Nasser.Alkhulaifi,Direnc.Pekaslan1,Christian.Wagner } @nottingham.ac.uk Abstract Entity Resolution (ER) pipelines often collapse ambiguity into early hard decisions: upstream Named Entity Recognition (NER) selects a single span and type, and downstream Entity Linking (EL) treats that choice as ground truth. This discards valuable information about the ambiguity of the underlying data (e.g., span boundary disagreement and type confusion), leading to brittle systems that fail unpredictably when faced with uncertainty in inputs. Therefore, this work presents a proof-of-concept for uncertainty-aware ER that treats uncertainty as native data that should be preserved and exploited throughout ER pipelines. We (i) capture uncertainty signals in the NER stage and (ii) leverage these signals into the EL stage to improve candidate retrieval under ambiguity. Using a BERT-based NER model augmented with two auxiliary span-boundary prediction heads, we apply Monte Carlo (MC) dropout at inference time to derive three mention-level proxy signals: the MC-averaged start-boundary probability, the MC-averaged end-boundary probability, and De Luca–Termini fuzzy entropy computed over the Begin–Inside–Outside (BIO) predictive distribution. These signals are used to adapt the fuzzy cutoff in candidate generation (CG) for EL. Because CG is treated as a blocking step, we evaluate retrieval recall. On the AnnoCTR dataset linked to the MITRE ATT&CK knowledge base, the boundary-aware and dual-signal fuzzy linking approaches improve Recall@10 from 0.6186 to 0.7966. The contribution lies not in an end-to-end optimised ER pipeline but in establishing uncertainty preservation as a viable and beneficial component of ER pipelines, enabling downstream EL to make better-informed decisions under uncertainty. 1 Introduction and Background Entity Resolution (ER) aims to determine when different textual mentions or records refer to the same real-world entity and to align them to a canonical representation, typically within or across Knowledge Bases (KBs) [ 40 , 3 ] . Accurate ER is a prerequisite for the construction and maintenance of high-quality Knowledge Graphs (KGs), since unresolved duplicates and incorrect merges propagate errors to downstream analytics, search, and reasoning [ 36 , 41 ] . ER for unstructured text is commonly operationalised as a pipeline: entities are first detected and typed via Named Entity Recognition (NER), then grounded (linked) to a KB via Entity Linking (EL), enabling richer structured context for subsequent retrieval and inference [ 3 ] . The upstream task of ER is NER, a natural language processing (NLP) task that involves identifying specific mentions in a given text and classifying them into predefined entity types, such as location, organisation, or person [ 18 , 27 ] . NER is a well-studied problem in the literature, with early approaches relying on rules, dictionaries, and statistical taggers [ 25 ] , whereas modern approaches predominantly use deep-learning-based methods [ 20 ] . Recent progress is driven by contextual encoders, particularly Transformer-based models [ 5 , 34 , 16 ] . Among these methods, span-based NER has become more prevalent because, unlike token-level sequence tagging, it identifies entities by scoring spans directly [ 37 , 38 ] . Spans are often represented using features derived from the contextual embeddings of their boundary tokens (first and last) [ 33 ] , typically produced by a pretrained language model (e.g., BERT [ 5 ] or RoBERTa [ 22 ] ). This span-level modelling tends to improve robustness to out-of-vocabulary words [ 8 ] and to missing or unlabelled entities arising from annotation errors [ 21 ] . The downstream task following NER in an ER pipeline is EL, which takes the detected entity mentions and maps each one to its corresponding entity in a KB, bridging unstructured language with structured knowledge for retrieval and reasoning [ 3 ] . EL is commonly implemented as a two-stage process: (i) candidate generation (CG), also known as blocking, which retrieves a set of plausible KB entities using the mention while reducing the number of candidate descriptions to be compared, and (ii) entity matching, which ranks these candidates to resolve ambiguity using a set of functions (e.g., description similarity) [ 26 ] . Recent neural EL systems attempt to reduce reliance on hand-crafted similarity features by learning dense mention–context and entity representations (often using attention encoders) [ 28 ] . However, they typically remain challenged by long-tailed entity distributions (i.e., a few entities occur very frequently while many others are rare) and KB incompleteness (including NIL/unlinkable mentions), and can be computationally expensive, especially when using cross-encoder scoring for candidate ranking [ 30 , 36 , 28 ] . Many ER systems still couple NER and EL through point decisions: EL CG is conditioned on the single best NER span and type, rather than a calibrated uncertainty signal over alternative spans/types [ 17 , 35 ] . This design is brittle because mention resolution is often underdetermined: small boundary differences change the mention string used for alias lookup and string matching during CG, and type errors can exclude otherwise plausible candidates when type constraints are applied [ 35 , 29 , 10 ] . The result is error propagation: early ambiguity becomes a hard commitment that downstream linking cannot easily recover from [ 17 ] . Uncertainty arises at multiple stages in the ER pipeline, and is therefore a meaningful signal, not just noise. At the NER stage, uncertainty typically appears as (i) boundary uncertainty (where the mention starts/ends) and (ii) label uncertainty (which entity type applies); recent works have explored uncertainty estimation and calibration for sequence labelling and NER [ 11 , 12 , 14 , 39 ] . At the EL stage, uncertainty is driven by the knowledge base and data distribution itself: aliases are shared across entities, descriptions can be sparse, many entities are rare and therefore poorly represented, and some mentions are simply unlinkable (NIL) [ 13 , 10 , 29 ] . In practice, CG involves balancing high recall against the introduction of irrelevant candidates through choices such as exact versus fuzzy matching, similarity thresholds, and pruning rules [ 29 ] . When upstream evidence is weak, however, a fixed CG strategy can either miss the gold entity or admit too many irrelevant candidates [ 10 ] . Uncertainty estimation for neural NLP has been widely studied, with Monte Carlo (MC) dropout providing a standard approximate Bayesian approach [ 9 ] . For structured prediction, recent works target calibrated confidence and uncertainty scoring for outputs relevant to NER [ 11 , 12 , 14 ] . However, comparatively little work uses NER uncertainty as an explicit control signal to adapt the EL CG policy, despite evidence that NER decisions materially affect downstream linking [ 35 ] . Therefore, this work addresses that gap with an uncertainty-preserving design. We (i) extract mention-level uncertainty signals from a BERT-based NER model under MC dropout (boundary confidence and entropy) and (ii) leverage them to improve CG in EL. By preserving these uncertainty signals rather than reducing NER outputs to a single point estimate, the downstream EL stage is better able to support informed decision-making under uncertainty. For example, candidate-retrieval behaviour can be adapted when boundary confidence is low or entity-type entropy is high, thereby enabling more appropriate downstream decisions such as linking, abstaining from linking, or flagging the mention for further review instead of forcing an early commitment to an uncertain match. The contributions of this work are summarised as follows: 1 1 1 The experimental code and materials required to reproduce the results are publicly available at: https://github.com/Nasser-Alkhulaifi/uncertainty-aware-cti-linking . • Extraction of uncertainty signals at the NER stage by augmenting the model with two auxiliary span-boundary prediction heads (start/end), followed by MC dropout to estimate predictive uncertainty. • Use of these proxies to adapt EL CG and improve gold-entity retention in a cyber threat intelligence setting (i.e., support better-informed downstream decisions under uncertainty). Description of the Treasury Nominal and Inflation-Indexed Constant Maturity Series Yields on Treasury nominal securities at “constant maturity” are interpolated by the U.S. Treasury from the daily yield curve for non-inflation-indexed Treasury securities. This curve, which relates the yield on a security to its time to maturity, is based on the closing market bid yields on actively traded Treasury securities in the over-the-counter market. These market yields are calculated from composites of quotations obtained by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. The constant maturity yield values are read from the yield curve at fixed maturities, currently 1, 3, and 6 months and 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 10, 20, and 30 years. This method provides a yield for a 10-year maturity, for example, even if no outstanding security has exactly 10 years remaining to maturity. Similarly, yields on inflation-indexed securities at “constant maturity” are interpolated from the daily yield curve for Treasury inflation protected securities in the over-the-counter market. The inflation-indexed constant maturity yields are read from this yield curve at fixed maturities, currently 5, 7, 10, 20, and 30 years. Back to Top Last Update: November 24, 2026 Back to Top
